speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members of the house for giving me an opportunity to make a statement in regard to the Congo situation, which is much in the thoughts and hearts of peace loving people everywhere in the world. I felt that it was proper that whatever information is available to the government should be given to the house, and that course will be followed not only on this occasion but in the days ahead.
In the last few days the Soviet aim has been the pursuance of its selfish ambition in central Africa and, in this pursuit, to paralyse the United Nations at a time when a supreme effort is demanded to prevent further deterioration in the crisis existing in the Congo.
I wish again today to reiterate support for the statement made by the secretary general in the security council yesterday when he replied to the Soviet charges. The United Nations organization was asked last year, first by the security council and later by the general assembly, to carry out certain responsibilities. There has not been that degree of co-operation required of member states for such a major undertaking. Quite apart from the complexity of the Congo situation itself, some members of the United Nations and especially the Soviet union have sought to frustrate the United Nations effort through direct interference in the internal affairs of the Congo. This mischief making has not prevented the same governments from calling on the United Nations to take action designed to serve partisan interests rather than to benefit the Congolese people.
In the face of the internal problems, the outside interference and the confusion and indecision on the part of member governments of the United Nations, the secretary general has sought to preserve and promote a United Nations policy which would lift the Congo situation from the conflict of interest of the powers seeking their own aims in Africa and would enable the Congolese people to solve for themselves their political difficulties.
In his statement yesterday Mr. Hammar-skjold demonstrated a full awareness of the direction in which his duty lies and a determination to continue on that course so long as he has sufficient support from the member governments. The main support must come from the African states themselves and from their Asian partners. If African progress and independence are not to become casualties of the cold war, the uncommitted states must see to it that the Congo situation is resolved in accordance with the best interests of Africans and of world peace. The United Nations can assist immeasurably in the pursuit of these aims, but the initiative and the strength of the United Nations assistance will depend on the cohesion of African and Asian support for the organization.
I might recall that at the very outset of the crisis last July I expressed this view in the house, and it has continued to be a basic consideration in the government's policy toward the Congo and toward the United Nations intervention there.
I trust that the secretary general will be accorded the support needed at this very critical time, from an overwhelming majority of the United Nations members. Now more than ever the United Nations must be given the authority it needs, and the required means, to use United Nations instruments in the Congo for the protection of civilians, for the promotion and enforcement of cease-fires, and for the reorganization of the Congolese security forces. There is need, too, for reassurance that outside interference, from whatever quarter, will cease. Only in these conditions can the United Nation hope to pursue its efforts to preserve the independence and integrity of the Congo, to maintain order there and to bring about the necessary reconciliation of all political interests in that country. I think that Canadians as a whole, and members of this house, will agree that the government should spare no effort to promote the attainment of these ends at the United Nations and wherever Canadian influence can be brought to bear effectively.
I might mention that the advisory committee for the Congo is holding an important meeting this afternoon in New York to consider a report by the conciliation commission, now in the Congo, which contains recommendations of a positive character. I might summarize those recommendations by saying

Statement on Congo Crisis that most of them are in line with the secretary general's plans for the Congo, including provisions for the establishment in general of a broadly based government.
I do not think there is anything further I can add at this time except to say that everything possible is being done in this connection by the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the house will have listened with great interest to the Prime Minister's statement, which underlines the seriousness and indeed the dangers of the situation in the Congo. I thought this was also done yesterday with great impressiveness by the President of the United States in his wise words on this matter.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the dangers we face in. this situation are threefold. There is a very real danger that the Congo will become a battleground in the cold war, and in doing so perhaps bring the, whole of Africa into the cold war, something which it has been the aim of members of the United Nations to avoid. The second danger is that, if things go wrong, the United Nations will be very gravely weakened, and the policies being pursued by the Soviet union and some of its friends at the present time are, it seems to me, in danger of having that result. Third, it may destroy a secretary general who has served the organization and served peace with such unselfish and patient distinction; and if that is allowed to happen it will destroy or weaken gravely the whole office of secretary general, whoever may be holder of that office in the future.
Surely, as the Prime Minister has said, what we should be doing in this situation is seeking for ways and means to strengthen, not weaken, United Nations intervention in the Congo, as was pointed out yesterday by the prime minister of India, in order to restore peace to that tragic land and build a foundation of order which would make freedom meaningful there. I do not know exactly how this can be done, of course, but perhaps one approach to a solution-this has been mentioned by others-would be to bring the Congo under some kind of trusteeship or something analogous to trusteeship by agreement at the United Nations, and then place in charge of the country as the administrator for the United Nations an Asian member, perhaps India, and, if that were the course followed, then we should back up the Asian country chosen as administrator with every kind of support, technical assistance, financial assistance, police assistance and political assistance. Perhaps this may be a way out of this difficulty. But if some way is not found 

not only will the United Nations be in danger but peace itself may be jeopardized.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in commenting upon the most interesting statement made by the Prime Minister with respect to the recent most tragic sequence of events in the Congo, I wish to say on behalf of this group that the former premier, Patrice Lumumba, was a person who without doubt, though possibly in the wrong way, strove to bring freedom to his people. Mr. Dag Hammarskjold, the Secretary General of the United Nations, has striven in every way, as we all know, to do his duty and carry out his instructions from that body.
Unfortunately both these persons have been victims of circumstances and a swirling of events over which they had little control. As far as this group are concerned, we believe that recriminations from any source would only serve to deepen the tragedy, create further chaos and make the solution of the problem more difficult and more distant. We support every effort that the government may make to use Canadian influence through the United Nations in order to strengthen, shall I say, the moral and material interests of the United Nations with respect to this very important matter.
Possibly in that direction we can not only use our moral influence along the lines suggested by the Prime Minister in the statement he read and along the lines suggested by the Leader of the Opposition. To indicate our sincerity and our willingness to put a shoulder to the wheel to the limit of Canadian ability and resources, possibly we might agree to increase our forces in the Congo if necessary or if called upon to do so, to send more food to the Congo, if necessary, than we have in the past and, if necessary, to provide further medical supplies.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I might make reference to a suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition regarding trusteeship, I would say that this suggestion has been made on other occasions. As he knows, it has its limitations and shortcomings.
I appreciate the words of both hon. gentlemen, and I think I should add this. Time is of the essence. The report of the conciliation commission which will be considered today provides for measures to stop the fighting and the drift toward civil war, the insulation of the Congolese national army from politics, the setting up of a training scheme under a defence council, and the meeting of all political leaders of the Congo to work out a new constitution along federal lines.
These recommendations come from a report made by a committee representative of the

Asian and African countries, and indicates the care and attention that has been given by those charged with the responsibility of being on that committee to meet the perilous possibilities inherent in inaction or uncertainty at this time.

The third item will be the continuation of the debate on the budget resolutions. If that debate is not concluded, we will carry on with it on Thursday.
This, sir, was confirmation of what the house leader had said on Monday and on the previous Thursday. I was therefore astonished when, without consultation with me and in my absence, the following exchange took place last evening, according to the Hansard record at page 2091:

Tomorrow we will take item No. 4 on today's order paper, the second reading of Bill No. C-69 dealing with the proposed railway line to Mattagami lake, which was discussed in the resolution stage yesterday.
In other words, what was announced last night was entirely different business from what had been announced earlier for the rest of the week.
My question of privilege, sir, is twofold. First, it has to do with advance notice of the business, which it has been the custom and tradition of this house to give to the opposition in order that they may properly prepare for debate. But there is another, and in my opinion more important and more serious matter affecting privilege. It is this. The Minister of Finance stated in the house on February 8, according to the Hansard record, page 1848, that we on this side of the house were delaying the progress of the budget resolutions. I should like to quote what he said in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Essex East seeking information about distressed areas. The answer was this:

Perhaps we may have some progress some day soon on these budget resolutions. We spent three days on one very short resolution last week. I hope we will have more co-operation from the opposition from this point on.
Then as found on the following page, namely page 1849, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition having to do with the policy of the government on chronic unemployment areas, the Minister of Finance replied as follows:
If the Leader of the Opposition will look at the answers I gave to the hon. member for Laurier when he first asked a similar question about a week ago, the hon. gentleman will find that I pointed out that I thought the house should pass on the budget before we attempted to deal piecemeal with some of the matters that I dealt with in the budget.
I say that these three statements by the Minister of Finance which I have extracted from Hansard of February 8 are a reflection on the opposition; and here we are at February 16, eight days later, and still the budget resolutions have not been discussed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    CHANGE IN ANNOUNCED BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier has raised a double-barrelled issue. I will deal with the first part which has reference to the business of the house as forecast. Had the hon. member for Laurier wished a change in the program for today, all that was required was a telephone call to me this morning suggesting that something should not be gone ahead with, and we might have made the alteration.
Each Thursday I have attempted to make a forecast; I started this practice last year and

Question of Privilege have continued it this session. For the benefit of all hon. members, not just those on the opposite side of the house, I have attempted to forecast the business for the following week as a guide for everybody in the house. However, I have been careful to state that this forecast is subject to change because the situation varies from day to day.
That is precisely what happened this week. It was not possible to bring forward the budget resolutions until Wednesday. Yesterday, I presume to the surprise of everyone, we did not reach the business of the house until a quarter after four, I believe it was, owing to the prolonged question period. After we dealt with one or two minor items there was little time left for discussion of the budget resolutions. Before the conclusion of yesterday's sitting a decision had to be reached as to what we would do today. That decision had to be reached just close to six o'clock. It appeared then that the house desired more time in which to consider the budget resolutions. Had it been possible to pass the first one yesterday, we considered it might have been possible to go ahead today with the one dealing with income tax. However, as the house appeared to desire more time on the first budget resolution it seemed wiser to shift to some other business, and that is precisely the decision I made.
I did not and do not feel myself committed to any forecast that goes a day or two ahead of the day on which we are going to sit. We are subject to adjustment from time to time as seems necessary. That adjustment is made on both sides of the house, Mr. Speaker. It will not be long before the hon. member for Laurier will be asking me to defer some piece of business because someone on his side is away and wants to participate in the debate. I will gladly do so in order to accommodate him, and the same statement holds true with regard to the corner group, as they called themselves yesterday.

Now, the reason I called second reading of the bill concerning the Mattagami railway was that I noticed there was general agreement on the other side of the house at the resolution stage. The hon. member for Laurier praised it twice in the course of his speech, and the hon. member for Villeneuve, who made a lengthy speech on the subject, spoke of the general advantages to be derived from that railway. I concluded therefore that there was a general desire to get ahead with the measure and that, consequently, we would proceed with it today.


That is the situation with regard to the business of this house. But, as I said last year, if the opposition does not like to have a forecast ahead of time I will revert to the practice followed by Mr. Harris when he was leader of the house, and announce the business for the following day the night before. I did not think that was very satisfactory in those days, and that is why I have adopted this other method.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Perhaps I might deal with the second part of the observation made by the hon. member for Laurier in the course of the speech he smuggled into a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman made reference to observations I had on February 8 as to the lack of progress with the budget resolutions concerning proposed amendments to the Customs Tariff.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that there are two resolutions before the committee of ways and means arising out of the budget; first, a short amendment to the Customs Tariff and, second, a series of proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act. We have now spent a total of four days on this small amendment to the Customs Tariff-a very short amendment, presenting an issue which could be discussed, surely, with reasonable brevity. I am not suggesting that anybody should abate or curtail his remarks, but I draw attention to the fact that this is one amendment and it is not a lengthy one. Despite all the time spent so far in committee we have still not been able to start in the committee of ways and means on the resolution relating to the Income Tax Act.
On February 8, as the hon. member for Laurier has pointed out, I drew attention to the fact that three days had already been spent in committee on the amendment to the Customs Tariff, and I deplored the fact that we were making such slow progress. Yesterday, another day was spent on this.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Peterborough asked a question, which appears on page 1972 of Hansard, with respect to serious advertising rate slashes by the C.B.C. The minister has been informed by the C.B.C. as follows. The corporation has not slashed advertising rates, nor does it engage in forms of merchandising and promotion which constitute rate slashing. Corporation selling practice is guided strictly by published rate cards, specifying rates for national network, national selective, and local retail business. speechtext:
I do not recall having received the particular resolution in question. I can assure the hon. member, however, that when it is brought to my attention it will be dealt with in the normal course of events. I might say this briefly, Mr. Speaker. Section 25(a) of the Unemployment Insurance Act specifies that one of the conditions of insurability is that a contract of service exists between employer and employee. Generally these are in the category of excepted employment.
It is not possible to make general observations covering all possible varieties of circumstances, since each case, Mr. Speaker, usually has its own individual peculiarities. the second reading of Bill No. C-69, respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of Quebec by Canadian National Railway Company from a point at or near mile 72 of the Kiask Falls subdivision in a northwesterly direction to a point in the vicinity of Mattagami lake.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the title of the bill indicates, authority is being sought to enable Canadian National Railways to build a 60-mile branch line from a point about 72 miles north of Barraute in the province of Quebec to a point near Mattagami lake and, as I said at the resolution stage, the cost of construction is estimated at $8,400,000 or $140,000 per mile.
The Mattagami lake area, Mr. Speaker, has been prospected off and on during the past half century, but it was only when modern geophysical methods of prospecting were applied in the 1950's that the presence of mineral deposits that could be economically developed was established. The first and most important discovery was made on a property which is now owned by Mattagami Lake Mines Limited, a company which is controlled by Noranda Mines Limited and McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited. Canadian Explorations Limited has also spent substantial sums of money in turning up large reserves of zinc and copper ore at that location.
The plans call for the installation at the mine property of a concentrate mill having a capacity of 2,000 tons of ore daily, and the construction in the St. Lawrence river valley of a refinery having a capacity of 200 to 250 tons of zinc metal a day. The company expects to begin production at this rate toward the end of next year.
The prospective traffic on the proposed line consists mainly of zinc concentrates, of which about 165,000 tons will move annually to the

mining company's refinery, and copper concentrates, 25,000 tons of which will move each year to the Noranda mine's smelter at Noranda. Other traffic made up of mine supplies and general merchandise will also be carried over the line. The Canadian National Railways have secured a traffic guarantee under which the mining company has undertaken to ship annually a minimum total of zinc concentrates during the first 10 years. The agreement contains a penalty provision in case the shipments in any year fall short of the guaranteed tonnage.
As I said when I spoke at the resolution stage, this project deserves encouragement as one that should improve the net position of the Canadian National Railways as well as contribute to the development of this important mineral and pulpwood area. As I mentioned when the resolution was before the committee, I intend to move that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where officers of the Canadian National will be present to give further particulars as may be required.

1.	That a select committee be appointed to consider the policy, operations and expenditures of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon;

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at any length on this motion, because it is the same motion that was before the house last session in the month of May. It is expressed in identical terms, and is a motion to reconstitute the committee which was set up last session. That committee had seven meetings. In its second report to the house it asked that the committee, or a similar committee, be set up in the next session of parliament so that it might continue its deliberations. I might just read the first sentence of the report. It appears on page 170 of the seventh report of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special committee on research and reads:
This committee recommends that it be reconstituted early in the next session of parliament in order that it may continue its deliberations.
Last session the committee heard from the national research council and spent about five meetings, I think, dealing with subject matters raised that pertained to that institution. I think the committee had in mind, had

there been time available, to visit some of the establishments of the national research council. There was not time to do that; consequently they terminated their discussion of the national research council and at a subsequent meeting heard from the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, who placed before them a comprehensive statement dealing with the activities of that organization.
Apparently the committee did not have time to go into that in detail; therefore its work was unfinished and it did not reach at all the third area of investigation, namely Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. Consequently this motion is now before the house in order to set up this committee again. By setting it up in February we will give the committee a chance to complete the work it started last session and investigate thoroughly the three areas that are indicated in the resolution.
I might say the committee asked that its terms of reference be enlarged when it was set up again, but we have brought before the house now the terms of reference as they were last year; they are in exactly the same wording.
Last year I pointed out the value of a committee of the house studying the activities of those three bodies. I indicated that I thought four years had elapsed since research had been considered by a committee of the House of Commons, and, in view of the great importance of research and the great importance of atomic energy, that it would be advisable to study the activities of those organizations.
Over a long period of years the national research council has performed a function in Canadian life that merits commendation, and during the last few years Atomic Energy of Canada has kept well in the forefront of atomic development in the world. I think it would be enlightening and informative for the committee to examine very closely the work of Atomic Energy of Canada to see what progress is being made. In addition to the research facilities which it has established at Chalk River, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is now in the process of expanding its activities, and later this year the first small reactor to deliver electric power to the Ontario grid will become operative. Within a four-year period a larger reactor, the CANDU operation, will become operative and will be delivering power to the Ontario grid. We feel confident that these two operations will prove of value in the use of uranium and heavy water as a source for the development of electric power.

Recently I was at Bombay, India, nearby which has been erected the Canada-India reactor based on the design of NRX at Chalk River and constructed with the advice and assistance of our atomic energy specialists and Canadian engineers, a joint operation between Canada and India, which was opened just last month by Prime Minister Nehru, representing India, and myself representing Canada. The Canada-India reactor is a very fine one. I would say it is the outstanding atomic energy reactor built in the world in the nature of its design and its appearance, and it will serve a very good purpose in the subcontinent of Asia to direct attention to atomic energy research and to train scientists in India, and I suppose in adjoining countries.
The future for the use of atomic energy for power is great. There are so many countries in the world that are looking forward to getting their power requirements from atomic energy plants that the pioneer work that is being done by Canada will likely bear fruit in the next few years. Therefore this is an appropriate time for a committee of the House of Commons to examine the very excellent work that is being done by our scientists and our engineers in the promotion of atomic energy and the development of atomic reactors. Then there is a third field for investigation by the committee, namely that of the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company, which did not have an opportunity to report to the committee last session.
This, Mr. Speaker, concludes my remarks. I commend to the house the setting up of this special committee.

international co-ordination of atomic energy knowledge. Speaking from memory, I believe Canada has contributed roughly half the cost of this reactor, and I believe the estimated cost at the beginning was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $35 million. We made our decision at a time when the United States had likewise decided to establish in the Far East an atomic energy installation in the Philippines.
I am sure we will all agree with the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) that this contribution of Canada toward bringing to India and to Asia a knowledge that was primarily discovered by scientists of the west is a contribution of which we will have every reason to be proud later.
