The minister has said that in setting up this committee an opportunity will be afforded to examine the work being done by Canadian scientists and engineers, and I think that is a very important examination for parliament to make in connection with a matter that becomes increasingly of such importance in the development of our world and national societies. We are the only country with atomic energy know-how and with an atomic energy installation that right

Research Committee
from the first decided that its atomic energy knowledge and installations would be used primarily for peaceful purposes. Neither the present government nor the former government has varied from that intention, and I am sure I express the hope of all Canadians when I say that I hope the turbulent conditions of our times will not prevent our adhering to that objective in the days to come.
I am sure this is a useful committee to set up and members of this party will play their part in giving responsible and careful scrutiny to the work of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited.
I have one final thought. The developments that have taken place in the national research council with regard to the setting up of a special section for medical research are a matter to which the minister did not direct our attention but one which I know he will regard with us as a decision of the greatest importance. Great discoveries are being made in many areas of scientific activity. In the field of medical scientific research discoveries over the past decade and a half have been of the greatest significance. It would seem to me that the decision of the director of the national research council and others to give a special status to medical scientific research is a wise move, and I believe that under the direction of Dr. Ray Farquhar-son that decision will stimulate medical scientific research, give added assistance to medical research in our universities, and generally make it more financially possible for many potential scientists to make their contribution toward the improvement of medical and health standards in this country.
The kind of pursuit envisaged in the setting up of the committee is one which hon. members will follow with only one concern, the advancement of scientific causes in the hope that in the days to come such advancements will be used primarily in the interests of furthering the causes of civilization rather than for the purpose of devising ways and means of destroying that civilization.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER POLICY, OPERATIONS AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a very great pleasure to be able to express the agreement of this group with the motion to set up a committee on research early in the session. Before I begin my remarks with regard to the committee, I should especially like to take this opportunity of doing what I have purposely refrained from doing up to now and pay my respects to the memory of my predecessor in the house, Mr. Gordon K. Fraser. I have not done so before because I wished to wait until I could relate his name to the area in which

he made his greatest contribution. All members now in their seats will know, of course, that he was chairman of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines at the time of his death, and possibly it was in this area that he made his most outstanding contribution. I know that his death nine or ten months ago was a tremendous shock to members of the house and I can assure you that it was a great shock to his constituents. Only a few weeks before I sat in the gallery as his guest and his respect for this house was evidenced in the fact that during the years he sat here he brought over 8,000 young people from the schools of Peterborough to Ottawa and entertained them here so that they could see the government of Canada in action. I can assure you that he will always be remembered as a credit to this house, a credit to his party and to his country. Indeed, it is with some humility that I attempt to follow in his footsteps.
In so far as the establishment of this committee is concerned, I think we must remember that it will give parliament an opportunity to investigate and to appreciate the work that has been done in this country in the field of research, especially since the second world war. Indeed, one might say that Canada has been in the forefront in this area of scientific research since 1916 when the national research council was set up. Perhaps it is as a result of this very important government agency that Canada's position is so high in this area of scientific research.
We in this corner are particularly enthusiastic since defence research has been separated from the national research council. Nearly everything which is done by the national research council, except in particular areas, is done in the name of peace. It is almost ridiculous now to say again that we stand at a fork in the road. One road leads to our complete annihilation, while the other leads to the end of poverty, sickness and disease throughout the world. I feel that years from now men will look back and realize that this country has done a great deal toward the solving of that problem. We have played a real role as a result of the national research council. It would take a great deal more time than is available at this moment to give the details of the work that has been done by the national research council in the various areas to which it has been assigned. It would take even longer to describe fully the fellowships, scholarships and grants which have been given, and the extent to which they have helped people in conducting research. I will, therefore, not go into that today.
Certainly one of the things which has been accomplished has been the bringing of foreign students to Canada to take part in this

scientific research, thus enabling them to take this knowledge back to their country. Surely no country can do more than this in contributing toward better understanding throughout the world. In addition, Canadian students have been able to go to other countries and have been given further opportunities for research. This interchange of ideas has perhaps made the men of science more internationalistic than any other group in the world. It would seem that the scientists are in the forefront of those who are concerned with making this a more peaceful world.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of its investigations this committee will come to realize the extent to which these agencies have given Canada a reputation second to none, especially in the area of atomic energy. Atomic Energy of Canada, of course, has had many pressures upon it. We realize that the resources of Canada are coming to an end or will be coming to an end during the next half century. We will be dependent, perhaps not in the foreseeable future but in the future, on atomic power. The fact that Canada has a nuclear reactor in Ontario is an indication that this nation is already looking ahead and is ready to begin the long process of converting to nuclear power. I am very proud of the fact that Canadian General Electric, a major industry in my constituency, has played a great role in this area of atomic research. Indeed, this private industry has supervised the construction and has helped to design this particular reactor, and has contributed some $2 million toward its erection. I think it is extremely important to remember that private enterprise is already willing to take an active part in this work.
I believe all these things point to the fact that this committee will provide parliament with an opportunity to participate in these most important developments. There are a number of problems with which I am sure all members in this house are particularly concerned. One of these problems is how nuclear power can be used safely and just exactly how we can get rid of radioactive material. These are things which must be investigated. It is to the advantage of Canada that she has begun her investigations early. I know that those members of this house who will be participating in this committee will find the work a great challenge.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER POLICY, OPERATIONS AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
In rising to speak to this motion, I do so on behalf of an area in Canada which constitutes about 40 per cent of our nation. When one considers that little is known about the northern sections of the provinces across the country, one can see that I am speaking about 50 per cent of the country. Northern research has been
Research Committee
sadly lacking, if not non-existent over the years. The investigations that were conducted by the mines, forests and waters committee in 1958 pointed up the serious lack of research in this area. I was rather hoping that when this committee was set up its terms of reference would contain a provision directing inquiries into the various factors which affect research in our northern areas.
At the moment the only research activities that are being carried on in the Canadian north are those which are being conducted by the Arctic institute which has established a station on Devon island in the Queen Elizabeth group. Then there is the Jacobson-McGill institute which has a station established on Axel Heiberg island. The stations which have been set up by these two units are run pretty well on private funds, particularly the Jacobson-McGill institute. Two other institutes have been established, one at the University of Alberta, which has been set up for research studies of the north. I believe this one is called the Boreal institute. Then there is one at the University of Saskatchewan which was established just last year or the year before, and I believe it is called the institute for northern studies. Of course, the Arctic institute finds its home in Montreal.
I feel that northern research is very important to the future development of Canada. I am sure the members of this house will agree on that score, particularly in the light of the northern development policy of this government. One should remember also that the United States is spending some $20 million annually on studies in the Antarctic. When considering the importance of northern research, one must keep in mind the fact that the Soviet union has approximately 100 Arctic stations that have been set up in that country for furthering these studies. These stations are in addition to the nine or ten floating ice stations, some of which are used as bases from which other scientific parties probe the Canadian sector of the Arctic. Since 1934 thousands of these travelling Russian scientific parties have probed the secrets of the Arctic to further their research. Indeed, they have come as close as 200 miles from the northern shore of the Yukon Territory.
I feel that the policy over past years regarding Canadian research in the Canadian arctic appears consistently to have been to do the minimum possible. The result has been that research has only been carried out when we have been pushed into it by other countries carrying out or wishing to carry out research in the Canadian arctic or by reason of some international program in which we had to participate such as the international

Research Committee
geophysical year or we have been pushed into it by the realization of how far we were falling behind other countries in northern research. I think that in view of the findings of the mines, forests and waters committees in 1958 and the evidence in support of those findings that there can be little doubt that we are sadly lacking in our research activities in Canada's north when those activities are compared with those of other countries, particularly those of the Soviet union.
To some extent this neglect of northern research was natural. The country is large and there are pressing research problems elsewhere with more direct application, some of which the minister has mentioned, and scientists are scarce. With the need to meet the immediate demands of a rapidly expanding economy there has been a reluctance to assign to the north any large portion of the country's scientific effort that the particular northern problems require. It is also a fact that in general Canadians have never been attracted to the north. For instance, a large number of Canadian missionaries do work in China while many missionaries in northern Canada are drawn mainly from Europe.
The benefits to be derived by the nation from an active program of northern research are many and varied. For the effective development of the north a major expansion of research is essential in my view. Without thorough and continuing research any development in the north is certainly to be more costly and more easily misdirected. Owing to our geographical location Canada is expected as a northern nation, an arctic nation, to take a leading part in any northern matter, whether it is civil or military. This is an obligation which Canada, as a northern nation, as a people of the north, cannot evade, but it is one which we shall never fulfil effectively without adequate research.
In a rapidly shrinking world, in the age of jet and space travel, our sovereignty in the north must be continually reviewed and strengthened. There is no more effective way, no means less costly and no means more intrinsically useful of strengthening Canada's sovereignty in the north than the conduct of thorough scientific field research programs and the publication of their results. I am not the only one who shares this view. Dr. J. Tuzo Wilson, who is professor of geophysics at the University of Toronto, in 1959, wrote a series of articles for the Telegram. During the international geophysical year Dr. Wilson travelled some 100,000 miles over the earth and during the 18 months of IGY spent some time in both the Antarctic and the Arctic. As set forth in the Telegram of January 7, 1959, he indicates the following views:

If there is one thing that the IGY has brought out, it is that we don't know enough about the Polar regions. Because of their special position they have unique geophysical interest and importance, but most geophysical theories have been built up upon observations made in temperate regions. In the IGY fresh information obtained especially in the Antarctic has shown that our ideas about wheather, aurora, magnetism, cosmic rays, nearby space all need modification. What is especially needed now is more information about polar regions and particularly about the Canadian Arctic. To gain this will require not 1 per cent of what has been spent on arctic defense and will save itself many times over when new developments are required.
I am sure that the Canadian government is quite aware of this and indeed it is already preparing new programs, but one feature of great importance is missing-the participation of Canadian universities on an adequate scale.
What are some of the research needs in the Canadian north? This subject can be divided into headings, the first of which I feel is technical and resource survey. The fundamental importance of detailed technical surveys appears to have been recognized in recent years and there has been a marked increase in survey work in the north since the second world war. Indeed, there has been an extremely marked increase in this survey work during the past five years. The program of air photography is of particular value as air photography, together with securing adequate geodetic control, is the only practical method of detailed mapping of the north and it was a startling fact which was advanced from the inquiries of the mines, forests and water committee of 1958 that at the present rate of mapping our country it will take 100 years to complete it. The present program and the related mapping activities appear to be somewhat lagging and it should be reviewed to ensure that it is keeping pace with requirements.
As well as mapping the arctic islands, there is a problem of charting the arctic seas. A program which I submit, from the information that was available to the committee in 1958, the Russians have almost completed. Here there is a tremendous volume of work to be done before charts comparable in scale and accuracy to those of more frequented waters can be produced. At the present scale of effort it would take some 250 years to complete this type of mapping.
The current interest in the oil potential of the arctic islands and the advent of submarines in polar waters are recent pointers to the necessity of greatly increasing hydrographic charting in the north. This can be done only as a long term program for which more special ships are essential. Here I feel the government is to be congratulated on the program that the Department of Mines and Technical Survey is carrying out in the polar continental shelf project.

Our future in the north is a mineral future. Minerals are likely to prove by far the most important resource of the north. I think that fact is well recognized. The mineral potential of the north is still unknown and the need for geological surveys is obvious. In a recent release by the bureau of statistics I note that in British Columbia from their 20 silver producing mines they produce only $300,000 more than the Yukon Territory produced with its one silver mine. It is therefore obvious that the economy of the country as a whole can be strengthened to the benefit of all Canadians if more such mines are operating. Only about one third of the Canadian north has been covered by geological mapping even on a reconnaissance scale and still more remains to be done in gravity and airborne magnetometer surveys. Without the geological surveys Operation Franklin, no commercial interest would have developed at this time in the oil possibilities of the arctic islands.
I cannot stress too much the importance of research in this field. Should we not be thinking of setting up an arctic research station for the purpose of investigating ice conditions, water conditions, surface conditions generally and subsurface conditions, as an assistance to those who are conducting the search for oil and gas in Canada's arctic islands? Little is known about the geology in these areas.
While recognizing the paramount importance of minerals as a resource, other possibilities should not be neglected. There is little detailed information on the water power potential of Canadian arctic rivers or of their seasonal variation in flow. Study of the potential of fisheries and wildlife and of possible conservation measures should receive increased attention. In other northern countries reindeer herding has proved successful. Experience in Canada was at first promising but has recently been disappointing. The reason for this probably lies in the lack of research into all aspects of the reindeer industry.
Research, too, is related to transportation. Transportation is one of the things most desperately needed for the efficient opening up of the Canadian north. I have already mentioned the need for hydrographic surveys. A related field is the study of ice formation and the distribution and forecasting of ice conditions. This is work at which the Russians have for many years been far ahead of the rest of the world. Canadian ice studies have recently been co-ordinated under the meteorological division of the Department of Transport. Most of the work contemplated, however, appears to lie in the simple reporting and forecasting of ice conditions. A promising 90205-6-134
Research Committee
area of research lies in the analysis of past records of ice and their correlation with meteorological factors.
Oceanography is of basic importance to submarine navigation as well as to fisheries research and has also far-reaching applications in other fields of science. I think that in 1958 the mines, forests and waters committee discovered that Canada had only one oceanographer in the whole of the scientific staff of the civil service and that we actually needed 35 as a minimum requirement. The program of Arctic oceanography initiated since the war and carried out to a large extent by the ship Labrador should be continued and expanded particularly in the channels between the islands of the Canadian arctic archipelago to complement the work of the Canadian polar continental shelf expedition which is now under way.
The joint arctic weather stations were established primarily for the purpose of forecasting and reporting weather conditions but they have provided a large amount of new data for research of wide interest. The programs at the stations could be further expanded, and Canadian sovereignty would be strengthened if the complete operation of these stations were taken over by Canada.
The application of recent advances in technology to the design and development of more suitable vehicles, aircraft and shipping for northern service would be of particular value to all northern activities. The transportation of the future in the north might well consist of truck trains with oversized or balloon tires travelling over the tundra and rocky country of the north to transport the ores to smelter and to market. Research into methods of icebreaking and the design of icebreaking vessels appears to be a most appropriate field for Canadian endeavour.
Owing to the events of the international geophysical year, geophysics have recently received considerable attention. The location of the north magnetic pole and the maximum auroral zone and the related implications for space travel and cosmic ray research make the Canadian north an area of exceptional geophysical significance which justifies a greatly expanded effort in geophysics. There are, however, other fields of pure research for which the north is particularly suitable. These include glaciology, arctic medicine, and physiology particularly in connection with cold adaptation and the interesting studies which were carried on during I.G.Y. by a team of doctors in the Old Crow region of the Yukon Territory from which some very useful results were obtained.
There is also a continuing requirement to collect and describe the natural history and material culture of the north and to conduct

Research Committee
archaeological expeditions, a field in which, I am happy to note, the government is now taking a more active interest. The national collections do not compare favourably either in size or accessibility with those of other countries.
There are certain special conditions in the north influencing construction and development and causing problems whose solution requires both pure and applied research. The presence of permafrost, for instance, is one of the most common of these problems; this permanently frozen ground has far-reaching effects on all types of construction. The nature of permafrost has to be fully understood if satisfactory construction techniques are to be developed. I think the government has found out, to its sad disillusionment what this problem of permafrost can mean. I remember one building which was constructed at Yellowknife which had a full basement. It was ten feet lower the following year because of the thawing out of the surrounding permafrost.
Another problem is the prevalence of biting flies which make outside activity intolerable. Here, fortunately, research in control methods has produced promising results. This is particularly important if we are to have any development of livestock farming in the Yukon. There are many fields of modern technological research which can overcome or reduce northern problems such as the long distance transmission of power, possibly by direct current and the prevention of freezing in harbours by means of compressed air or by nuclear devices.
The current changes in the north cannot fail to have a profound effect on the native peoples. In recent sessions of the Yukon and Northwest Territories councils and elsewhere grave concern has been expressed that the impact of civilization and the consequent destruction of native culture is resulting in a serious and rapid decline in standards of morality. The situation demands a comprehensive program of research in social anthropology, to determine and define the problems facing native peoples under these conditions and to recommend measures to alleviate their difficulties of adjustment. Without these studies a heavy and continuing price will be paid in relief and rehabilitation measures as well as in human suffering which might have been avoided.
I mentioned the universities and so did Dr. Wilson in his series in the Toronto Telegram. In any plan to increase scientific activity in the north the universities must play an important part, both in the actual conduct of research and in the training of northern scientists. Scientists are hard to get at any

time but without sufficient government support we shall not get them at all. Scientists who are willing and able to go to the north but who cannot afford to outfit themselves stand in need of an organization with the necessary funds to back them. The government should therefore, in my view adopt the policy of supporting these institutions by grants in aid to such as the institute for northern studies in Saskatchewan in order to assist and encourage their research activities.
It has been suggested that some universities should specialize in northern studies. This appears however to be a restrictive policy. Northern research is so important to Canada that in my opinion all universities should be encouraged to undertake northern studies, and the need only becomes greater in view of the increasing demands which are being placed on the funds required to run our universities throughout the country. I appeal for government support in this field. The most effective way of providing this encouragement would be by making grants available to universities for programs of northern research. In this way certain faculties at universities could build up their capacity to undertake northern research and to provide trained scientists. This should be initiated immediately in order that university faculties might be able to orient their activities with the object of making grants on an increasing scale to reach about $1 million a year within three or four years. To serve both government and university scientists, laboratory facilities are necessary in the north itself. These should be on a modest scale-and I do mean modest scale -providing the minimum accommodation necessary for scientists to carry out such laboratory investigations as cannot be carried out in southern Canada.
Dr. Wilson suggests such an establishment at Hazen lake on Ellesmere island. The defence research board has a laboratory with facilities for defence research at Fort Churchill. I suggest that these facilities be made available for civil research. In addition, two laboratories, one in the high Arctic in the arctic islands and the other in the western Arctic, are necessary.
The government has taken a step in the right direction in providing in the estimates this year, I believe, sums to provide for the establishment of a research laboratory at the new settlement at Inuvik in the Northwest Territories. It will take about two years to complete even this small station.
I should like to conclude these remarks by quoting from an editorial entitled "Time to

Make the Arctic Ours" which appeared in the Kingston Whig-Standard, of March 6, 1959, and which reads:
It appears that we need to do more survey work in the area-*
Of northern Canada-
-and that the only really safe position is that of actual occupancy. It has been admitted by the minister of mines, Mr. Comtois, that very little has actually been done to increase the pace of our Arctic research. The government now has plans for more activity and there is at present an expedition on the continental shelf.
It seems strange that, with all the discussion of our sovereign rights during the past few years, the government has not done the obvious things in the north country. We talk a good deal about how important the whole area is to us, both economically and strategically, and yet we have undoubtedly neglected to act as if we were determined to keep trespassers out. We may wake up some day and find that this situation has been exploited by some other nation and that we have on our vital back doorstep a most unwelcome- and permanent-squatter.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the setting up of this committee. I am very happy that this committee is being set up again this year. This, in my opinion, is a very important committee. In so far as it relates to the national research council I think it is important for parliament and for Canada to know what is being done in that organization. My own private opinion is that good work is being done and that while its activities are carried out within the confines of scientific laboratories the results of these activities should be communicated, not only to those who are indirectly affected but in particular to those who are directly concerned.
In so far as the activities of this committee are concerned with atomic energy it is important to know what progress is being made in a field in which Canada was a pioneer. In the atomic age and in the age of automation research in its widest sense expresses itself in our standard of living, in industry, in labour and, in fact, in every segment of our national life. I believe, too, that we are at this time passing through a stage when research in all its forms is more important than it has ever before been in the history of our country.
Last year's committee was set up late in the session and there was not time to do all the things which hon. members of the committee would like to have seen done. The operations of a research organization must of necessity be complex and time is required to obtain a detailed knowledge of its activities.
While the time at the disposal of the committee of last session was insufficient, I believe that the committee, under a very able chairman, made a very good beginning. This year, with the committee being set up earlier 90205-6-1344
Research Committee
in the session I would hope that it would be able to give attention to those areas of inquiry which could not be considered last year.
I was fortunate enough to be a member of the committee last year. In the meetings we were able to have last year I came to the conclusion that the amount of work this committee is required to do is so great that it might be worth while if the committee were divided into two parts, one part dealing with the national research council and research in general and the other dealing with atomic energy and related research.
I do not know if the minister proposes to have this committee operate every year but I think it might be a good idea if in one year the committee would deal with the national research council and research in general and the following year deal with atomic energy, Eldorado Mining Company and other aspects of our atomic research.
We all know that research in the field of science has expanded greatly in Canada during the last 40 years. The national research council, established in 1916 under the name of the national advisory council for scientific and industrial research, had during its first year less than 20 employees. Last year the total of scientists, technical employees and service staff was approximately 2,600 and this figure does not include those employed in defence research and atomic energy.
The committee was able to see last year that the national research council has not only increased in size but has become increasingly important in the quality of its scientific investigations and the importance of these investigations has been recognized, not only in scientific circles in our own land but in every country in the world in which any worth-while research is being conducted.
During the third meeting of this committee last year the members were discussing the increase in the circulation of Canadian scientific journals. During this discussion it was learned that in the month of May 1960 the circulation of these journals totalled 10,000, 4,000 in Canada and 6,000 in foreign countries. Dr. E. W. R. Steacie, president of the national research council, used the distribution of these journals to illustrate the growth and importance of Canadian science. I should like to quote from page 121 of the evidence given before last year's committee, where Dr. Steacie in referring to the growth in Canadian scientific journals, said:
Really, this is just a reflection of the fact that Canadian science has come ahead. Thirty or forty years ago there were just the odd small groups which were internationally well-known. There has been a very big increase since. The net result is that scientifically, rather than being in the backwoods we have now become one of the important scientific countries in the world-

Research Committee
This statement coming from a man of Dr. Steacie's stature, from a man who enjoys such a distinguished reputation in scientific circles both inside and outside Canada, should not be allowed to pass unnoticed and should indicate to parliament and to the Canadian people that the quality of Canadian science and research warrants our attention and support.
Last year when the minister referred to the setting up of this committee he said that the research complex consisted of government, universities and research. That may be one of the reasons why Canadian science has become so important as it is. It is because of this group of three which is doing such a fine job of research in Canada. I do not think that scientific research, fundamental research, or any other kind is ever going to be very important in any country unless the universities are able to make the greatest contribution possible.
As far as industrial research is concerned, I believe that we should take a much wider view. I know that industrial research may not come directly under this committee, but one thing I would suggest is that at some time or other this committee take a very wide look at research as it exists all across this country. At the moment I believe we are in a position where we cannot afford to have research in countries which are our competitors ahead of research in our own country. We need more products, different designs, not only for the people of our own country but for exports, and these new products and designs can be arrived at only by industrial research.
In years gone by not a great deal of research was done in this country and even up to recently much of it was done either by parent companies outside of Canada of subsidiaries in Canada or by large companies. In fact, even in 1959, 72 per cent of the total amount of money spent on industrial research was spent by companies whose liabilities were over $50,000,000. In this country we would not expect small companies would make a very large contribution to industrial research. Obviously they would not have the facilities to do so. An electronic microscope, for example, properly placed, would cost somewhere in the vicinity of $70,000 to $80,000. An infrared machine would cost in the vicinity of $15,000. These are expensive pieces of equipment for small industries, with the result that most of our industrial research has been done by the larger companies in conjunction with, of course, the universities and the national research council.
There are those who contend that we are not spending enough money on industrial research in this country. In the year 1960

the amount spent on research in Canada was about 1 per cent of the gross national product. This figure of 1 per cent is compared with the United States where the amount of money spent on research is about 2.74 per cent of the gross national product. I could not agree with this particular comparison for the simple reason that the United States government gives great support to defence production and to industries engaged in defence production, much more so than we do in Canada. I think a much better comparison would be to compare our situation with the situation in the United States in 1954. If we were to do that-and we would then be excluding much of the money which has moved into defence production-we would have the amount of money spent on research in Canada as one per cent of our gross national product and the amount spent on research in the United States as 1.4 per cent. When it is viewed in this manner it is obvious that we are spending per capita approximately the amount of money that the United States is spending. I am not trying to argue here that we are spending enough. I still think there are many things to be done in research in Canada and they can only be done by the government and industry making contributions to research in general and to the universities in particular.
I suppose most people have heard something about a little disagreement going on now between industry and the national research council. The national research council says that industry is not alert to the things that are being developed by the national research council, and the industry says that the national research council is not producing those things which can be easily manufactured. Here is a question which this committee might take the trouble to look into and see whether the needs of Canada, in so far as research is concerned, are being met by the national research council, by industry and by the universities.
I do not suppose that the suggestion which I am going to make now would have very much acceptance, but if this committee were to get a broad view of research as it goes on in this country I think it would be necessary not only to discuss what goes on with the national research council, with industry and with atomic energy and so forth, but what is done by other departments of government that have research departments. I am only talking about the other departments of government bringing in their research activities. I am not talking about discussing estimates, or anything like that. If that were done, then this committee would get an idea of what goes on not only in the national research council, in industry and at the

universities but it might also get an idea of the research that is being carried on by other departments of government. I know that this research in other departments of government is taken up in the committee to which the estimates are referred, but in this particular instance I believe that if departmental research were taken up in this particular committee it would be possible for the members of the committee to have a broader view of what actually goes on in research in this country.
I suppose it is a little bit difficult for any country to retain all the scientists it produces, but I believe we must make an effort to provide the proper equipment, the proper environment and the proper incentives for those Canadians who become expert in the field of research to remain in their own country and work for the good of their own country. I believe that can only be done after giving to research in all its phases the assistance which it deserves.
I am not going to make any comments now about the idea that has been talked about recently, namely the research community, but I believe that the research community has much to commend it and I believe it is really important to industrial research in this country. Therefore, as we increase our research in this field we shall be also retaining well trained scientists within the confines of our own country.
In the field of atomic research there are those who believe that here again we are spending too much money. I do not believe this is true. In 1960 the per capita expenditure by the Canadian government was $2.25. In the United States it was approximately $1 per person. Another measurement of how much we are spending on research and atomic energy as compared with the United States would be to compare the annual expenditure on nuclear power with the total annual value of sales of electricity. This figure for Canada would be 5 per cent; the figure for the United States would be 1.5 per cent.
I think there are two reasons why we in Canada should take nuclear research very seriously. First, Canada pioneered in this field and we should make every effort to maintain this advantage. Second, the time is not too far away when we are going to be able to construct small nuclear power plants which will be able to produce electric power efficiently. This will be of tremendous advantage in many parts of our own country, particularly the north, and certainly these units could be sold in many other parts of the world.
Canada should not spend on nuclear research at the expense of other forms of investigation but should spend enough to
Research Committee
preserve and protect our interests at home and abroad. Some attempt should be made to determine what Canada should be spending. I think that would be a very good question for the committee to examine.
When we were discussing the report of the committee last year I thought that we were not spending enough money on medical research, and I believe that here is one field where a good deal more attention could be paid. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) mentioned a few moments ago the transmission of electric power. I referred to this last year because I have a direct interest in the matter. We in Newfoundland have in Hamilton falls a great potential source of electricity. If that electricity has to be transmitted by the usual high tension alternating current method we are not going to get the amount of power from that source that we might otherwise get. I believe that here is a field of investigation-some other countries have taken up the matter-where we might investigate the possibilities of transmitting over long distances large amounts of power by direct current.
There are many other fields of investigation in Canada that need to be examined. There is no necessity of my saying any more now. I do say that I am pleased to see that the committee is being set up again. I think it has a lot of work before it and my main recommendation is that the committee be divided into two parts, one to undertake investigation of the national research council and research in general and the other to examine into research in the field of atomic energy.

Mr. Speaker, I always listen with interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) on topics of this type because I always think he makes a most thoughtful contribution to the debate. I rise to express my wholehearted support for the motion because I believe that in view of the importance of research to the Canadian economy it is very necessary that the house and the country be well informed concerning the policy, operations and expenditures of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited. When we realize that there is a total expenditure of approximately $30 million I think this indicates the scope of the work undertaken by these organizations.
Before proceeding to deal with the question I rose particularly to discuss, I should like to mention the fact that in a quite well known report some time ago it was suggested that the staff of the national research council and

Research Committee
such organizations be brought under the terms of the Civil Service Act. As far as this group is concerned, we would oppose any suggestion to implement that recommendation regardless of the importance and the high standing of the gentleman who made the recommendation. We in this group think it would be most unfortunate to take a step in that direction. It would undermine the spirit of free inquiry and the spirit of scientific initiative which we believe it is most necessary to retain if the staffs of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Company are going to make the greatest possible contribution to research at this time.
I rose particularly, Mr. Speaker, to deal with an article that appeared in the Financial Post of January 28.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he proceeds to another subject? Would he make it clear that the suggestion about the staff of the national research council did not come from anyone in the government?

I am sorry if I did not make that clear. I thought everyone in the country was so well aware of the suggestion and had such knowledge of the details of the report that they would know the report to which I was referring. I am referring to a report made by Mr. Heeney, I believe, with respect to the civil service. I accuse the government of a great many delinquencies, but in this case, regardless of party, we all agree that they are not guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you.

I am very interested in what the hon. member has said and prima facie I am inclined to agree with him. However, if I were suddenly asked why I feel that research in this department is entirely different from research in the Department of Finance I would not be able to answer the question. Perhaps the hon. member could enlighten me.

I think research in the Department of Finance at the present time would be research related to government policies and possibly involving influences of that kind; in other words, surely it would be mathematical and mechanical research. I am referring to scientific research where the staff must be free to develop their lines of inquiry and their scientific investigations in a way that is unrelated to government policy.
Having leaped that rather low hurdle, I will now proceed with the matter that caused me to rise because in recent days I have been restraining myself very much, and I am sure

the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) will give me full marks for that. I have reference to an article in the Financial Post of January 28, 1961 which has caused some concern to persons interested in the work of the national research council. While I am only a humble backwoodsman living a more or less peasant farmer's life under normal circumstances, I do read the Financial Post to find out what industry and those who control the wealth of this country are doing other than the control that is retained by governments, both federal and provincial, which in my opinion is increasing almost every day.
Then you say that research of this type is in a category by itself.

Quite right. I say that as a member of parliament and not as a scientist. I find that the Financial Post is a very responsible and reliable paper with respect to the economic questions that come before us in Canada and that are multiplying every day, not particularly because of the deficiencies of any government or individual but because of the nature of the development of our country which is becoming so complex and complicated. In my more or less contemplative moods, Mr. Speaker, when I look around me and realize the endless problems we face from day to day which I quite admit are not going to be solved entirely by legislation, I can well understand why the Buddhists build monasteries in the Himalayas.
I want to deal with this article because I have had some correspondence about it and as this paper has a wide circulation the article has caused some concern. After reading the editorial I will deal briefly with a few comments made by persons on both sides of the controversy. The article appears in the column, "The Nation's Business", and it is headed, "Make Our Ideas Earn Our Keep". I have tried to do that all my life, Mr. Speaker, and have always been successful. The article reads in part as follows:
Top Ottawa scientists, including such able and distinguished men as president E. W. R. Steacie of the national research council, charge that Canadian businessmen are unalert to, and largely unaware of, the value of scientific research. They say Canadian industry is neither bold nor imaginative about developing new, money-making processes and products created by N.R.C. scientists.
They strike out particularly at "lack of initiative" among Canadian subsidiaries of U.S. companies.
This is an indictment of some gravity. It comes from men who spend over $30 million annually of the taxpayers' money to keep Canada abreast of scientific innovation in this fast-moving world.
These criticisms, as might be expected, have brought heated protests and countercharges of "prevarication and fabrication" from businessmen.

It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that there are persons who use rather strong language outside of this house as well as in it.
There is little point in declaring either the scientists or the businessmen wholly right.
But there are some hard facts to consider.
Canada allots only 1 per cent of G.N.P. to research and development v. the 2\ per cent spent by the U.S.-yet we try to live and prosper like Americans. Less than one third of the Canadian research spending is done by business, the rest by governments. The greatest part of all privately sponsored research, 70 per cent, is done by the really big companies only-those with annual sales of more than $50 million.
It is true that Canada has often taken the easy way out and let the U.S. do much of its research for it-and Canada has benefited. It is also plain that the relatively small Canadian market simply isn't big enough to make every top idea which national research council comes up with worth developing, if business even knows about it.
This editorial goes on, and I am quoting it at length because I think it is very well written and informative.
Twenty six Chances at Success
It is a known fact that for every national research council invention developed and sold by a Canadian company, another invention has been turned down in Canada only to be licensed abroad, produced abroad, and imported into Canada from abroad.
I want to insert at that point, Mr. Speaker, the remark that this is after the Canadian taxpayer has paid for the research that produced the invention.
But neither business nor the scientists will make yards for Canada by shouting about the past. Let's, instead, see what can be done about improving communication between science and industry. This cannot be achieved by industry having only its own scientists keep in touch with national research council. It takes an industrialist to transform a feasible idea into a marketable product.
That is very well said.
If industry is more prepared to examine the potentials in national research council work, then national research council has some responsibility for keeping industry informed and enthusiastic about its projects.
More immediately, let's see what can be done about the 26 new patents on the national research council list which the scientists say are immediately feasible for Canadian development. That is where the profit in this controversy lies.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, the various persons concerned have comments to make. There is an article here by Mr. Terence Robertson which is headed, "Our Patents Going Abroad: Research Storm Blowing Up". I have noticed that the articles by Mr. Terence Robertson are usually exactly written; they are not written for sensation. Anyone who has followed his articles must have noticed that he must do a great deal of research himself because his figures and his facts are accurate. He says:
There's a big debate brewing in Canada. Does Canadian industry make full use of discoveries by Canadian scientists?
Research Committee
Some scientists this week boldly charged that industry fails to develop the results of government-sponsored research-[DOT]
Then, later in the article, he says:
Industry leaders retorted heatedly to the charges. They blame the scientists-particularly those of the government's national research council-for failing to tell industry what they are doing. Industry leaders also insist that scientists don't understand marketing problems, or the kind of sales potential needed to justify development.
Then the various persons give various illustrations of inventions that have been produced and what has happened to them. They are being sold abroad, and so on. Then, after the charges made by industry, various members of the national research council reply. Dr. Steacie says, and I quote:
Although there are encouraging signs of increasing enthusiasm on the part of industry, I must admit that on the whole they don't show much interest-certainly not as much as we would like.
Then Dr. Mackenzie, who I might mention is very well known and a member of a famous Canadian battalion, the 54th Kootenay battalion-I cannot lose an opportunity to mention that fact-has this to say:
I blame Canadian industrialists for being unalert to the opportunities presented by the work of the national research council and other government scientific departments.
The various representatives of industry and the national research council present their views concerning both sides of this question.
I believe it is a good idea to have this debate because it brings to the attention of members certain facts. I am sure most members of this house were unaware, as were the people of the country, of many of these facts. I suggest that in addition to the proposed routine examination which the committee will undertake of the policy, operation and expenditures of the national research council and these other organizations, in the light of this article and the difference of opinion that exists there should be a most detailed inquiry into the situation and the senior staff of the national research council as well as the leading industrialists should be asked to come before the committee to give their views. I think it is very necessary that we secure the facts so that, as a result of that inquiry and the discussions that will revolve around it, we can do as suggested in the editorial, remedy the situation as soon as possible.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to make one other suggestion. I feel that the value and scope of the work of the national research council and these other organizations is insufficiently known to many Canadians. I have often talked to people about this question and I find they are unaware of the work of the national research council,

Research Committee
the provincial research councils and the research that goes on in universities. I do feel that the national research council could perform a great service if it established a public relations department so that Canadians generally would be informed of the work carried out by this organization under the sponsorship of the parliament of Canada. The students in universities, and even in the high schools, could be kept informed so that they would have some idea of what is being done in this field, especially as it related to the development of our economy. I believe that in so far as the high schools are concerned, it could be related to the local circumstances of the community in which the high school is situated.
I find particularly that certain sections of smaller industries are very ill-informed as to the value of the work of the national research council and these other organizations as it relates to developments in their own industries. I suggest, therefore, that the council would be well advised to have a public relations department to improve its public relations, to disseminate more information as to its activities generally. The scientific reports that are made are excellent for the people who use them, but I am thinking of publicity that would just inform the public of Canada generally as to the work of the council and these other organizations. Some of this information could be provided by means of pamphlets. I think, too, the council could secure the co-operation of the press and some national magazines if there were some procedure worked out whereby these reports would be given under a certain heading in these publications, a heading such as, "What Research Is Doing for You". I am thinking of something in the popular style used by the magazine Popular Mechanics. I have seen excellent work done by organizations of this sort, which are largely unheard from so far as the Canadian public is concerned and whose achievements are unsung and untold in many quarters.
Before concluding I suggest that is one thing that should be done in order to get a wider recognition of the value and scope of the work that is being undertaken-I refer to its value not only to our times but to the young generations that are growing up- in the development and the improvement of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this motion to set up this special committee to examine into the operations of the national research council and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Hon. members will perhaps appreciate the fact that these days I do not always rise to
[Mr. Herridge.j
support something brought forward by the government. As a matter of fact, I have occasion to differ sharply with them on most of the things they bring forward. However, today I wish to commend the minister for bringing forward at a relatively early stage of the session this motion to set up this committee.
I regard the motion as merely a continuation of the authority granted last year to a committee to examine into this subject, and I believe that is the way in which the minister intended it to be taken. The committee was set up last year with the same terms of reference but regrettably it was rather late in the session when it was set up and there was not an opportunity for it to do the work it had hoped to do. It was obliged to forgo almost completely the opportunity of examining into atomic energy matters.
The history of these committees is rather interesting to me. In 1949 for the first time a committee was created to examine into the operations of the atomic energy control board. It will be recalled that at that time there was a great deal of reason for security in the committee's examination. However, there was no practical difficulty in the workings of the committee. Indeed, on that occasion I think the house looked on this as a nonpartisan matter. It is interesting to note, as I had recalled to my memory only a few moments ago when I turned up that reference in the library, the first speaker on the opposition side on that occasion made it quite clear that he was supporting the motion and gave his reasons. That spirit has been continued throughout these committees and I hope my remarks today will be in keeping with that spirit.
Then in 1950, the next year, a committee was created to examine into the operations of the national research council. Then in 1953 a special committee was appointed to examine into the operations of both. Then in 1956 a similar committee was appointed. I am sorry to say that I may have mislead the house. The committee in 1953 examined into the operations of the government in the field of atomic energy. The course of proceeding up to that time had been to refer to the committee one subject or another, namely the national research council or the atomic energy subject. Then in 1956 a special committee was set up to examine into the role of the government in the field of non-military research and specific reference was made to both the atomic energy field and the national research council. The reference last year followed that practice of combining both subjects as does the one this year. I do not know that it matters a great deal which method is used. A great deal of work

is indicated. It is not too important which method is used but a great deal of work is required in order to cover both subjects in one session.
The committee members were kind enough in the first four committees I have mentioned to appoint me chairman. I think I can say that in my experience as a member of the House of Commons I have not sat on any committee in which closer co-operation was granted to the chairman by the members of the committee than was granted in those four committees.
I hope the chairman of the committee last year could say the same thing if he were here today. Certainly for my part, as a member of the committee I felt that the chairman conducted the proceedings of the committee in a way that was wholly agreeable to all hon. members sitting on that committee. Every opportunity was given to the members of the committee to examine into the subject matter as thoroughly as they wished. The feeling of fairness and the spirit of co-operation among committee members were most satisfactory. Within the limited time at its disposal the committee was able to accomplish a good deal of work. However, regrettably, the time was much too limited having regard to the scope of the subject matter referred to it.
The committee last year dealt a great deal with the national research council. Before leaving that aspect of the subject I want to place on record what I regard as an extremely significant fact, namely the high calibre of persons who have been chosen under succeeding governments to head the national research council from its inception. This is a fortunate thing for this whole enterprise. I think the high achievement they have been able to record has been due in large measure to that fact.
There is another subject that is very much in my mind, namely the relation of the national research council to industry. I feel that the work of the national research council must be kept well balanced as between research in pure science and research in applied science. I believe the balance between those two matters must be maintained. I hope that at no time will the research council be forced into a position in which an abnormally large percentage of its work will be directed to the field of applied science. I believe that is a field that must be occupied partially by them but largely occupied by industry and outside agencies.
In that connection may I say this. I hold the view that the government must reexamine the matter of corporation taxes or taxes applied to industries in this country in order to ascertain whether we should go
Research Committee
further in making tax adjustments for research. In my view we must make appropriate tax adjustments for the work of industry in the scientific and research field.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member about to conclude his remarks?
I hope to conclude my remarks in about one minute, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We might go on for two or three minutes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is only a matter of a minute or two more, perhaps the house will agree.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. That is a subject that probably can be discussed more appropriately when we are dealing with the budget and the estimates rather than on the motion to set up the committee.
Then there is to be considered the field of atomic energy. We are at a critical stage of its development. I look forward with eagerness to examining into the exact state of the development in relation to the production of power-I refer to the use of nuclear energy for the production of power-and its relationship to industry. If we can develop an additional economically feasible source of power in this country at this time it will do much to strengthen our whole economy over the years ahead. I am looking forward to that opportunity of examining the subject. It may well be that we are at the stage at which we may be obliged again to adjust some of our taxation policies in order to take cognizance of the new developments in that field and of the rapidity with which they have come about.
Without further remax-ks, Mr. Speaker, I want to express my approval of this motion to set up the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

No, Mr. Speaker; it is six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
speechtext:
I rise to support the resolution. I doubt whether the value of research as such to the progress associated with modern living is appreciated, at least consciously, to the extent that it should be or to the extent that it merits. Therefore I should like to begin by paying a tribute to those who spend their lives

Research Committee
in studious research in connection with the gathering of knowledge and whose unspectacular work has made possible the spectacular progress associated with this age.
In most phases of human endeavour the hallmark of the twentieth century has been progress and this is true particularly in the scientific field, in transportation, in medicine, in the production of food and in many other directions. It is to the production of food that I should particularly like to refer and I wish to deal with one foodstuff especially, that is, fish.
My interest is, of course, obvious. In the riding which I have the honour to represent many of the people are fishermen, and the waters off the coast of Labrador and northern Newfoundland are very rich in fish. The question naturally arises: are these resources being utilized to the best possible extent, and is modern technology being applied to the production and processing of fish? I should like to point out that the fisheries of the Atlantic provinces are important not only to the Atlantic provinces themselves but to the whole of Canada. I should like to raise the question whether these fisheries can be augmented so that the whole of the Canadian economy might be strengthened.
Closely allied with this object is the question of research. Lest I should give the impression that research has been neglected, I hasten to say that such is not the case. Over the years much work has been done with regard to fisheries research. A lot of time and money has been expended, and able men have made and are making a study of fish their life's work. It goes without saying that for these dedicated scientists and technicians all of us have a great deal of respect and a great deal of appreciation. We appreciate what they are doing and what they are trying to do. I should like to point out the need for an extension and an enlargement of the research work being done in this field. My personal opinion is that the job these men are trying to do is made more difficult by the lack of the necessary funds and the necessary help.
A great deal of information has been gained already, but the field is wide and the possibilities are many. More and more knowledge is needed on which to base an expansion of the industry, and the search for knowledge is one which must go on continuously and unrelentingly. 1 might mention a few of the subjects about which more information is required. There is, for instance, the movement and behaviour of herrings; the need for knowledge to enable us to predict where they can be found. Then again, why does the cod, the basic bread and butter fish of the Atlantic waters, sometimes disappear from the areas where it is usually found? This happens
[Mr. Granger.!
periodically, and it happened last year. Codfish practically disappeared from whole sections of the coast. There must be a reason for this, and there must be some way of predicting in advance whether or not such a phenomenon is likely to occur, I might add, when it does occur it means well nigh tragedy to the people involved. This year there is a lot of arctic ice off the coast and it has been suggested that in consequence the fishing will be good. Is there, in fact, a relationship? This is something which might be looked into.
The means of increasing production are important. Obviously it would be ideal if the catch per man could be increased and if at the same time the value of the catch could be increased. I shall not, of course, discuss the economic side of the question but I should like to point out the need for research into the whole fishing question.
There is one matter which I raised before in this house, the great need for artificial bait. Every year many thousand quintals of fish are left uncaught because fishing communities are short of bait. I believe that this factor alone would warrant intensive research into the development of artificial bait which could supplement the bait that is usually used.
There is the matter of improvements in cold storage facilities with a view to making better, cheaper and lighter units. There is also the falling off of the salmon fishery and the need for research into the reasons why this has occurred and the possibilities of improving and increasing the number of streams where salmon may breed.
In addition there is the matter of research into the mechanics of fishing and the processing of fish. Important steps have already been taken in this field. I think of mechanical aids for the splitting, filleting and drying of fish but too large a segment of the industry still depends on primitive methods which are really out of place in our modern day economy and in the highly competitive fields in which both the fishermen and the trade have to operate.
These problems are not new and have already been given considerable attention but I should like at this time to emphasize the need for giving these matters even more attention and I urge that these problems be treated with greater urgency.
The need for developing the north has already been mentioned by several hon. members as has the subject of the possibilities which long range power transmission open up for the north. If the resources of the 6 million or more horsepower on the Hamilton river were made available a large part of Canada and perhaps areas outside would benefit greatly.

In a nation such as ours with an expanding population, holding our own is not enough. Holding our own is merely inviting disaster. It is almost a matter of life and death for us to keep ahead technologically of the rest of the competition. We must advance ahead of the times. The only way to do this is to devote more time and money to patient and dedicated efforts in the field of research.

Mr. Speaker, before this motion is carried I should like to make a few brief remarks on the question of forming a committee to look into the operation, expenditures and policies of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. In making these remarks I want only to emphasize the growing need we have for increased research in this atomic age. I should like to mention a few fields where more research might result in the development of certain new industries in our country in general and in my own district in particular.
I know of the wonderful job that has been done in recent years by the national research council as was pointed out by previous speakers this afternoon and evening. I know, too, the council has a significant contribution to make in the years ahead. By way of example I should like to mention the fact that research into the peaceful purposes of uranium could be very important for our country and the future of our uranium industry.
Not long ago, if my memory serves me right, we were informed in this house about the important development that had taken place in respect of alloys developed for steel which would require the use of uranium or radioactive material. This is one example which indicates the importance of research in a new field. We are in a new atomic age and I think it is worth while that the government assumes the responsibility through the work of the national research council of developing means of assistance for our new metal industries such as uranium.
There are also other metals that have been found in abundant quantity in Canada in recent years in respect of which research could play a very important role in terms of the future development of these deposits. We know, for instance, that in Canada we have on the north shores of the St. Lawrence the world's largest deposits of ilmenite which contains titanium and which is in increasing demand for the construction of jet motors and other things. We also have large deposits of columbium and tantalum. One is near North Bay and the other of
Research Committee
which I am thinking is near Montreal at Oka. Columbium and tantalum have been known for many years but their use is relatively new and it will increase in years to come. Research will play a vital role in determining increased uses for these metals.
I now want to briefly mention a new metal about which we have heard with increasing frequency in recent times. One is always tempted to say a "new" metal, but of course these metals have been known for many years and have come into use only recently.
I refer to lithium. Large deposits have been found in northern Manitoba, northern Ontario, and particularly in my district in northern Quebec where it is believed the largest known lithium deposit has been located. As a matter of fact this resulted a few years ago in the building of the first lithium mine by Quebec Lithium Corporation.
To illustrate the importance of research in that particular case, let me say that the mine was hoping to start production and had a contract with an important United States firm but they were not too sure what process they should use. Up to that time the process used was what we call a dry process method which had been used in the United States. Apparently that was the one that was most advantageous. Quebec Lithium Corporation, however, decided to look into the problem, had its metallurgists study the situation and through the co-operation of the Quebec department of mines laboratories succeeded in developing a new process. They used a commonly known method which was not previously believed suitable for the extraction of lithium ore. They used a wet process well known throughout the mining industry but adapted it in this case after careful research to enable the flotation of the spodu-mene crystals in order to make a concentrate of lithium that could be sent to those industries which require this metal. We hope the demand will increase in years to come.
I might say the company is controlled by two mines, East Sullivan and Sullivan Mines, which in turn are headed by a well-known French Canadian. I might say this is almost an exception. He is one of the few French Canadians who have succeeded in the mining industry and built up a mining empire of that kind. I am referring to Mr. Pierre Beauchemin. I pay tribute to him. It might be thought that this gentleman had done enough. Instead of retiring he kept right on and now the company in question has built a refinery which is the first lithium refinery not only in the province of Quebec but in Canada. This group is very aggressive in trying to find new methods and new

Research Committee
processes for the extraction of lithium metal, a relatively new metal so far as use is concerned.
I feel the national research council would do well if it could enlarge the use of lithium in the years to come by intensive research. The research program could also be extended into other metals such as molybdenite. Research programs should be intensified to find new uses for the metal. This research program should be conducted into the use of all of our base metals, and it should be intensified in co-operation with private companies and industrialists. If new uses were found for these base metals it would increase their sale, since they are produced in large quantities in our country.
This afternoon the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggested that the national research council would do well to have public relations men to publicize their work to the industries and to the public in general. I think it is a wonderful idea. I think the suggestion should be adopted, but I would go even further. I suggest that the public relations men of the national research council should intensify their co-operation with industry and thereby bring about new processes for the use of different materials in the country. This would be beneficial to industry and to the people of the country.
I wish to read a few headlines which appeared in the Wall Street Journal in reference to different new problems which have arisen in recent years as a result of the development of the atomic age. One headline reads:
Hydrogen age sets challenge for chemicals.
Another one is as follows:
Nuclear energy developments to spur new prospects for chemical energy.
A third reads:
Revolution in textile manufacture.
Further down the page we have another headline which has to do with an important industry in our country. It reads as follows:
Pulp and paper industry shows marked growth.
I recall that I was a member of the committee on mines, forests and waters in 1959. This matter came up when we made a careful study of our forest resources. At that time we had witnesses from different companies who mentioned that their companies were doing much research in developing new uses for different products and finding new markets for them. I should like to emphasize the fact that more co-operation should take place between the national research council on the one hand and companies across Canada on the other which are doing their own research.

Industrialists should be encouraged to do research in different ways, either through collaboration directly with the national research council or in other ways. In that way research programs could be stimulated all across Canada.
Before I resume my seat I should like to emphasize the fact that lithium ores are found abundantly in northern Quebec. As I mentioned before, the deposits there are believed to be the largest in the world. There are also large deposits in northern Ontario and in northern Manitoba. I believe that this metal will become the fuel of the future for jet planes. Experiments are being carried out to that end. I hold in my hand a research magazine which has a very detailed article in that regard. I will not read it because it would take too long. Borax and lithium mixed together have been used, and in time they will revolutionize the fuel used in the airplanes of the future.
