Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel) for his speech delivered in tip-top English, following an excellent example set in this house.

Hear, hear.
(Text):

Research is such an O.K. word right now that to come along with any strictures and warnings is sort of like being a pagan among the vestal virgins, but I have the feeling that we have rather gone overboard for the magic of the word "research" in the last couple of years. I was at a parliamentary committee a couple of years ago that went very strongly for research. Now we have the new Department of Forestry, Mr. Speaker, that is primarily to be concerned with research, and where-ever I go in the forestry circles and talk to woods managers and people in the business I find that they are a little bit frightened of the word "research". They do not mind basic research in their fields, but they are very much interested in what research has been done since the war which has some kind of practical pay-off.
I realize there is a split between applied research and basic research, and it seems to me the national research council in particular does a magnificent job in basic research. I often wonder whether the success they have is in that particular field which spills over to a degree into the applied research that they have, for example, in the field of snow and ice mechanics and whether there may not be a lesson there for the other departments of government such as forestry, mines and technical surveys that they might profit from.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
It seems to me the basic reason why the national research council is probably more effective in research than the ordinary government department is that the scientists there are not civil servants; they do not have the strait-jacket of the civil service arrangement. It may be that the national research council is extremely good because there is a flexibility and an income and outgo of all scientists from all over the world on a continuing, regular basis in their establishment, and so they have a plastic, wide open kind of organization where there is a considerable amount of discussion and cross fertilization with other parts of the world.
My own impression of the forestry research, for example, that is going on in this country under the federal department is that to quite an extent it is divorced from the over-all research that is taking place in the world of forestry. I think the committee might very well consider looking at the research programs of some of the government departments with an eye to seeing if the national research council could not be an example to them.
The last point I want to make relates to a story that was told me by a scientist in Ottawa. He said, "You know, over the years members of parliament become curious about research programs and critical of the money being spent on research." He said, "You can always stop them quickly; all you have to do is to get a bunch of members of parliament into a party and take them off to Chalk River or some other place with big laboratory facilities, let them be impressed with a bunch of dials, gadgets and counters that they do not understand, let them meet a few men in white smocks and they all come away saying it is a marvelous place, these scientists are wonderful people who are doing a great job, and in the end their curiosity dies down." The point of the story is that apparently this is a way that scientists can take baying parliamentarians off the track. I think there is a great deal to this.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is hardly fair to the scientists. Perhaps the hon. member is speaking in a jocular vein but I wonder whether that is quite fair to the scientists who are charged with responsibility for our national research.

I do not know whether it is quite fair to the scientists but I think it is certainly fair to the members of parliament. This is the point I should like to make about the committee and its work and I may say I discussed it with the chairman of the committee last year and he felt very strongly about it. It is almost impossible for a member of parliament to make a real contribution to the work of this committee unless he is
prepared to spend a great deal of time studying the whole research field, not so much from the point of view of becoming an expert in any sense in one field but in order to understand the problems of research as a whole. I would commend to all members of this committee the kind of study, shall I say, that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has given to agriculture and soybeans in his specialization-
I cannot do everything.
-although I might be thought flippant if I brought him into this field.
My time is limited.

I might suggest the wonderful study that the hon. member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. McGee) has made in the development of efficient commuter trains to serve certain sections around Toronto. The point is that the members of the committee can only do a good job in examining the research establishment of the government if they spend a considerable time in study, perhaps an inordinate amount compared with that required for other committees. I know that one reason I never tried to be made a member of a committee was that I considered it was a little bit too much work.
Motion agreed to.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Rea in the chair.

Citizenship-
49. Citizenship branch, $808,322.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. lady will no doubt recall that last year I expressed some misgivings about some of the expenditures under this item and even went the length of suggesting that consideration should be given to the consolidation of this branch and the citizenship registration branch. The hon. lady will also remember that I had something to say about some of the publications of the Canadian citizenship branch and in particular the magazine Citizen which is still being published.
I have not looked up the record and I may be wrong but if I remember rightly the hon. lady said there was a considerable demand for this magazine and I asked if there was an effective demand in the economic sense, in other words, whether enough people in the country were willing to buy this magazine at a price which would pay for the cost of producing it. I have looked through the most recent number and while I certainly do not

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration take exception to anything in it I would think that if we are going to spend money on publications at all there are other publications in this country on which it might be spent, even perhaps by giving financial assistance to magazines of more general interest, which would perhaps do more to promote real Canadian citizenship than the maintenance of "kept" journals of this description.
I know it is very easy to ask me what I did about this when I was minister and I admit that the answer to that question is a very short one, that I expressed misgivings and did very little else. I felt at that time, when we were having immigration on such a very large scale, that I should give my primary attention, which I did, to the immigration branch and also to the Indian affairs branch. But I did feel that a good deal too much of the money of this branch and of the time of the members of the branch were taken up with activities which, however praiseworthy they might be, would in my book not rate very high on the list of priorities for the expenditure of public money.
As a result of the establishment of citizenship courts in those areas of the country where the largest concentrations of recent immigrants exist, it does seem to me there is even greater reason for considreing carefully and, indeed, taking action on the suggestion I made last year that these two branches should be consolidated. I do think there is a place for liaison officers who would perhaps be a little like the pensions advocates on the board of pension commissioners and who would help immigrants with their difficulties before the court, in preparing for the court and other matters of that sort. However, I think this whole activity ought to be tied much more closely than it is to the actual potential citizens and not be so diffuse and general as it is.
I admit that in the light of all the estimates the amount involved is not very great but that can be said, of course, of a great many other expenditures. My own feeling is that when all is said and done an expenditure of $800,000 is still quite a lot of money and that perhaps some of that could be saved. I am not suggesting that the officials should be dispensed with or anything of that sort. I think there are other useful things that have to be and could be done.
However, this is probably one of those areas which will be examined by the Glassco commission when it gets around to it. Perhaps as a former minister, having expressed these rather vague misgivings, I would be well advised not to go any farther at this time. I want to make it very clear that I am not reflecting in any way on the members of the staff. I am not reflecting on anyone. I am
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
just questioning in my own mind whether, in view of the many demands on the taxpayers' dollar, some of the things that are done in this branch are really high enough in priority to warrant the expenditure.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. So far as the language classes are concerned, they warrant spending everything on them that can be spent profitably from the point of view of reducing the period in which newcomers to Canada suffer from the disability of not being able to speak one or the other of the official languages. In this connection, when the hon. lady replies later, I would be interested to know whether she has now been able to establish any better relations with the authorities in the province of Quebec or whether she has made any attempt to establish any better relations with the authorities in the province of Quebec, with a view to having closer co-operation in the language classes than it was possible to get at an earlier time. I know nothing about this. It is just a query. I have felt for a long time that more would be desirable there if it could be accomplished. There is no question whatever that the department, wherever it could avail itself of the ordinary adult education facilities that exist in a province, has always sought to do so and I would hope would continue to do so.
There is one other question of this character that I should like also to put to the hon. lady. There were several experiments conducted in the teaching of languages. I think we would all be interested to know what success there had been with some of the research in which the department was interested a year or two ago. I may have asked that question last year. I think I did. If I did, and there is nothing new to be said about it I do not want to take up the time of the committee.
There is one other thing that I should like to say before I sit down. I think we all realize that one of the most important elements in the satisfactory integration of newcomers into our society is that there should be a sympathetic attitude toward these newcomers on the part of the rest of us who are here. This is one of the things this branch of the department has sought to promote through voluntary organizations of all kinds. I would not suggest for a moment that I would like to see that kind of activity discouraged; far from it. However, I have some doubts, myself, about whether the attempts that have been made-some of them of course have been exceedingly well meaning-to use the facilities of the branch for the purpose of promoting closer relationships between the two groups of older Canadians are really perhaps as badly needed as some

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
of these other activities are. I think that is something that is really looking after itself rather well at the moment.
I said a moment ago, and I want to repeat, that a sympathetic, reasonable and honest attitude and a respect for the facts is very important if we are to have a proper integration of the newcomers, a proper understanding of the relationship between recent immigrants to this country and those who have been longer in the country. I cannot help but think that one of the best ways to promote that would be to have a really intimate relationship between the courts and the liaison officers of this branch, to the point where they really are a single organization.

Mr. Chairman, before embarking on a sort of hatchet job on what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had to say earlier, I should like to concur in everything he had to say about the importance of a sympathetic, reasonable and honest attitude, as he described it, on the part of those of us who are already here toward those who have come here recently and will come in the future. I think perhaps this attitude is very appropriate at this particular time of the year since brotherhood week is almost upon us. Speakers right across this country will be reminding the participants in these brotherhood week activities and those who attend the brotherhood banquets of the absolutely vital necessity of emphasizing this particular aspect.
I have not had as much opportunity as I would like to have had to examine some of the documents that are put in the hands of new Canadians, such as the one to which the hon. member referred. Certainly I would be unhappy if some of the prouder aspects of our history in this realm were not mentioned there. I am thinking particularly of a reference to Ezekiel Hart and the well known story of that early example of tolerance and understanding on the part of the French Canadian citizens of Three Rivers. If this story and others like it are not contained in these pamphlets outlining and underlining our proud and successful history in this regard, I would be very much disappointed.
I should like to return now to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Before I came to the House of Commons I heard a lot about the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and some of the difficulties he had encountered. Of course, I read and heard a great deal about the various activities of the cabinet of that day. The impression I gained, and apparently it was shared by a large number of Canadians
in 1957, was of fumbling and bumbling and perhaps not coming to grips with some of the issues that had to be met.
I should like to describe in his own words, as he described to us a few minutes ago but from a slightly different approach, his attitude to the department. He said he had misgivings; he had his doubts about this particular branch. What did he do? Apparently he did not do anything except indulge in these misgivings and doubts. He went on to say that we must not dismiss anybody. We should not misunderstand; let us not spend any less money. He was not criticizing anyone in particular in the department. He went on to point out that $800,000 is a lot of money, an important amount of money. Having said all that, giving his background and offering this great experience he had in the department to the present minister, the Glassco commission or anybody else who was interested, he then embarked upon the advocacy of another measure which involved the expenditure of additional money.
Oh, no.

The hon. member says, no. I would remind him that just a short time ago he was advocating the expenditure of an extra sum of money on language classes. The hon. member shakes his head. I think Hansard will bear out the validity of what I have said.
Spend existing money on it.

I have gained a greater understanding of some of the reasons why the hon. member used to encounter some difficulties when he was a minister. This was his typical obvious pattern of doing nothing, having doubts, not criticizing anybody, not firing anybody and ending up by advocating additional expenditures. It is no wonder that he encountered difficulties.

I should like to correct the hon. gentleman. I think he has made a good point. However, I did not in fact, suggest spending any more money. I suggested that some of the money now being spent would be better spent on lanugage courses.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 49 carry?
No, Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. lady wishes to speak.

I think I might give out a little information on the basis of the questions asked and the comments made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In so far as the organization of the department is concerned, of course that is one of the matters that is under active consideration at the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration present time in line with the investigation being made by the Glassco commission. With regard to his comment on the language classes I might tell him that about 50 per cent of our expenditures go to the language classes and we think we are making progress. I cannot tell him what the result is of the research that went into the matter of teaching and texts. We received copies of the new textbooks from the authors only last fall. This is the first year in which they are being used. We shall have to assess their value at the end of this year.
With respect to teaching French in Quebec may I say this. My hon. friend will recall that the other night I said we expect to open the first of such courses in Montreal in the latter part of February and, depending upon the success we encounter there, we hope to proceed to open other classes.
Are these classes given by the department or by provincial or local authorities?

They are sponsored
classes. I think I have covered most of the questions which were asked except with regard to the publication of Citizen. I might say that this year for the first time we have a sizable subscription list. About 25 per cent of the copies issued are now being subscribed for at an appropriate fee. We hope the subscription list will increase to the point that it will possibly pay for itself eventually.

I do not want to take up any time if someone else wants to speak first, Mr. Chairman. However, there is one rather less pleasant matter about which I want to say a word merely for the record. It is not in criticism of the hon. lady or of the department.
I said earlier that I felt that the business of integrating newcomers in Canada depended to a great extent on a proper understanding and a proper appreciation of the facts of the situation. I am going to draw to the attention of the committee a statement made by a minister of the crown as reported in the Niagara Falls Review of October 27, 1960. I do not think it contributes much to this kind of understanding, concord and harmony that I would have hoped every member of parliament would wish to have in this field. I refer to a report in that newspaper of a speech made by the hon. member for Bellechasse- and I regret very much that he is once more not in the house-the Secretary of State, in another by-election in which he was as successful as he was in the one in Labelle. This quotation from the Niagara Falls Review for October 27, 1960 is in quotation marks.

I intend to read just the quotation itself and then to make one or two observations on its content.
I have before me-
This in quotation marks.
-figures from the Post of November 9th, 1956, which show that under the Liberal government of that era Canada had a total of 292,000 unemployed despite a lot of surplus money. That same year machinery was set up that Canada was the victim of mass immigration with 280,000 immigrants reaching these shores in 1957.
Then the report continues in quotation marks.
"We inherited a Liberal policy in this regard and the Progressive Conservative government has been taking steps to correct it ever since. For their mass immigration policy," continued the Secretary of State, "we have instituted a selective immigration program which drastically reduced the number of immigrants to less than half that figure in 1958. That year only 124,581 immigrants were allowed into this country and that was chopped by 20,000 in 1959. Under this selective policy only those immigrants who can be absorbed into our economic set-up are allowed."
There are one or two comments I want to make about those statements which were made by the Secretary of State and which appear in quotation marks in this report. In the first place, I assume that by the Post the hon. gentleman meant the Financial Post. I do not know of any other newspaper called the Post that would be apt to have these figures. I therefore went to the library this afternoon and I looked up or tried to look up the Financial Post for November 9, 1956. I find there is no such thing. The Financial Post in 1956 appeared not on November 9, but on November 10. However, thinking this might be just a mistake in the day, I looked at the microfilm of every page of that newspaper and nowhere could I find any reference whatsoever to unemployment.
I then looked up the official figures of unemployment put out by the dominion bureau of statistics for the month of November, 1956. I have them here in my hand at the moment. The D.B.S. figure from the labor force survey for persons without jobs and seeking work on November 12, 1956, was 135,000. That is a long way from 292,000. However, a year later, on November 16, 1957, five months after the government opposite came into office, I find that the figure was 292,000. At the time about which the hon. member was speaking, namely the autumn of 1956, at the time the decision was made to admit the Hungarian refugees to Canada, there were 135,000 persons without jobs and seeking work according to the D.B.S. figures. As everyone recognizes, for the month of November that figure is just about the equivalent of full employment. It seems to me that this fact ought not to be misrepresented

by a minister of the crown. Moreover, a minister of the crown describes the admission to this country of Hungarian refugees in these terms:
That same year machinery was set up that Canada was the victim of mass immigration with 280,000 immigrants reaching these shores in 1957.
I am sure that the hon. lady would not like to be associated with that kind of description of the policy of admitting Hungarian refugees which the present government, as I have always been happy to give them credit for doing, carried right on after they came into office as long as the need was there. I give them full credit for that action. However, it seems to me that it is not right for any member of this government, even though he was not in the government or was not associated with it at that time, to say that Canada was the victim of this mass immigration, when one thinks of the plight of these people and when one thinks of what they were trying to do that caused them to be in that plight, that these people were fighting to free themselves from a communist regime. Yet the Secretary of State chooses to describe them in that fashion.
I think that is entirely unworthy of any member of this house and particularly of a minister of the crown in the government of a Prime Minister who in 1957, in this same area, in St. Catharines I think it was only a few miles from Niagara Falls, said he would triple the immigration the Liberals had developed at that time. I am also struck by this extraordinary sentence: "Under this selective policy-" that was chopped down, to use the unattractive verb employed by the Secretary of State. I quote again:
Under this selective policy only those who can be absorbed into our economic set-up are allowed to enter.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
When I have finished.
Was that speech made in French or in English?

I point out that when the Hungarian immigration started there were 135,000 people without jobs and seeking work, and when the hon. gentleman was talking last October about only those immigrants being admitted who could be absorbed half a million Canadians were out of work. How he reconciles that sort of thing with this kind of statement is something I would prefer to leave with hon. ladies and gentlemen on the other side of the house.

I have no comment to make on the charges which have been levelled against one of my colleagues by the
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration hon. gentleman who represents Bonavista-Twillingate, because I have never seen the alleged statement in print nor have I had the opportunity to assess its significance, but when it comes to the question of the Hungarian influx, if it might be called that, may I say that I was in this house at the time and I recall the situation quite well. I am sure that in all fairness the hon. member will be glad to admit that there was not one dissenting voice from any side of the house concerning the proposal that this scheme be put into effect.

I quite agree with the hon. lady and I thought I made that clear in my remarks, but if I did not make it abundantly clear then I want to make it clear now. There was the most complete support from the official opposition and, indeed, I think from everywhere else in the house. I recall no opposition in the house to that policy and I was always proud of the fact that it seemed to me all Canadians had responded in a wonderful way to a challenge which I regarded as a challenge to the whole free world.

Item agreed to.
50. Grants to organizations as detailed in the estimates, $40,000.

I see this vote comprises a grant of $15,000 to the Canadian general council of the boy scouts association, $15,000 to the Canadian council of the girl guides association and $10,000 to the boy's clubs of Canada.
While these are really only token grants toward these organizations, we are, at least, very pleased to see them continue. I think the work which these organizations are doing at the present time is, if possible, more important than ever. I intended to have some further remarks to say but I will simply suggest that consideration be given to increasing these grants if at all possible. I know it is easy enough to get up in the committee and suggest that grants be increased, and I know the difficult situation which exists today, but I do think that these are three organizations which we should do everything we properly can to assist, particularly in view of the challenge they are meeting today in providing these services to the boys and girls of Canada.

Item agreed to.
47. Departmental administration, $1,001,840.

I was not here, and perhaps I should have been, in order to raise a couple of questions relating to immigration. I do not know whether the minister has answered these. I am not going to give any general talk on immigration or make any general

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration contribution to the debate, but I should like to ask the hon. lady some questions regarding immigration from Italy and some details of the backlog of applications that are now in hand. That is the first question. The second one is how the department is adjusting to this increasing backlog in order to take care of it administratively and, third, whether the minister can give us any indication how long the backlog is likely to exist at the present rate at which people are coming to this country.

The backlog as of the end of 1960 was 63,341 all of whom, with the exception of 23, were sponsored cases. It stands to reason that so many applicants present a somewhat terrifying administrative problem. This has piled up over the years. When persons come here they bring their relatives. We are making every effort to bring wives and husbands or dependent children- to try to give them priority-but the problem still exists. However, with respect to some of these cases which have been on the books for a couple of years we feel that possibly the original sponsors may not be quite so eager to have them come out, so in order to ascertain the true state of the situation these cases are all being investigated to ascertain if the original sponsor is still in a position to receive his relatives.

I thank the minister for that last information. I was going to suggest that as she was probably aware members are constantly being approached with the suggestion that they check into what has happened in connection with various applications. I was in the office of one Canadian of Italian background a few weeks ago and he had a file there of several hundred cases of people who had applied and had received their initial letter of response and nothing had so far developed. In many cases the time lag had extended over the two year period. I not only think it is worth while from the department's point of view to remove the applications that may now be invalid because the parties are no longer anxious for them to come here, but I also think the department might consider some kind of reply to people who are waiting and still anxious to bring the people over.
I do not know whether the minister can make a reply now to that suggestion, but why should people have to wait 18 months to two years without any indication as to why, perhaps, the medical examination has not taken place or why people have not been called to the offices in Rome?

I think their relatives over there can give them the required information in correspondence. I might point

out to the hon. member that if we have to write 63,000 letters twice a year it is going to bog down the position even further. Whenever an application is made for up-to-date information on the state of any case we find out immediately and answer as quickly as possible.

Is there not, I will not say unfairness, but is there not something not quite right about accepting so many applications? You give these people the right-is it not a right or a privilege under our immigration set-up-to bring their relatives in. They take this as an important part of their prerogative of living in Canada. They know of the delays and hear of the backlog building up and there seems to be no end. It is three years since I became cognizant of the backlog and its increase.
I will admit that immigration has tended to tighten up in the last 18 months but that was not so several years ago. If the government for some reason is following a policy designed to use an administrative holdup to keep immigrants from Italy entering Canada, I am wondering if it is not time to be perfectly honest and frank with the Italian community in Canada and the Italians in the old country.
I am not trying to stir up a hornet's nest. I know the minister encountered some difficulties some time ago over new regulations she introduced that would have affected immigration from Italy but it seems to me in the long run the new regulations she had to withdraw would have been more fair than the present system of dragging out the matter. I will be interested in her comments on that.

Mr. Chairman, the action that has been taken has been taken and I do not intend to comment on it but to answer my hon. friend's other remarks, I do not think you can call it a slow-down when nearly 21,000 came in last year.
To put it more directly, is there any prospect which the minister can foresee of the backlog being reduced within the next two years which we will say is the life of her administration in one sense?
As I told my hon. friend a few moments ago, we are investigating the sponsorship of all these cases. There may be some of them who are no longer interested in bringing forward their relatives.

I have one other question referring to a specific case concerning which I do not wish to generalize. I refer to people from Portugal who entered the country illegally and voluntarily turned themselves in.

They had purchased improper visas and after turning themselves in and appearing before the appeal board were deported. Even though I took an interest in the appeal I have no quarrel with the decision of the minister to have these people deported but I wonder if the minister can say if this permanently kills the possibility of those people having another chance to come to Canada?
Just to elaborate, it is my experience that these people lived in a state of anxiety and because of the particular milieu in which they have grown up they tended to take for granted as part of their way of doing things that they would pay so much money to someone and in return get a visa. It turned out that the visa was illegal and in a sense they were trapped and betrayed by their own ignorance. I know that ignorance is no excuse before the law and they were properly deported but is there any opportunity for those people to make legitimate applications to come to Canada and is there any likelihood of their applications being fairly considered?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot give a general answer to that question. I would have to know what the case was and determine just how serious were the charges. In some cases the deportation is not held against a person in the event of his subsequent reapplication to enter the country legally. However, I could not make a general statement without knowing the particulars of the case.

Can the minister say if there have been any changes in the regulations governing the coming into Canada on a temporary basis of musicians and other entertainers? If there have not been can the minister briefly tell us what is the situation?
My reason for raising this matter is because a few weeks ago a furore was created in Vancouver when one of the newspapers published a report to the effect that the minister's department was taking what was described as a dead aim at imported entertainers. The report said if there were not some new regulations there was going to be a stringent enforcement of existing regulations concerning the length of time entertainers could stay in Canada. The suggestion was made that they could stay here a maximum of four weeks and would have to leave the country for four weeks before they apply to enter again.
According to the report, musicians would have to put up a cash bond of $100 and other types of entertainers a cash bond of $300. A number of people drew this matter to my
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration attention and the report created a furore as the minister will understand. I would be interested in the minister's comment.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there has been any change. Of course, each of these groups of entertainers is judged on its own face value. We have to determine if the group is a bona fide entertainment group, whether it has a contract of employment in Canada and whether it is putting Canadians out of work. There are a great many angles to this matter.
I do not think the payment of a cash bond is usual for the average group of entertainers entering Canada. It seems to me I recall something about this particular instance but I cannot remember the details. I would be glad to inquire into the matter and give my hon. friend a complete report on the particular case which he mentions. There seems to be many things which happen in Vancouver which do not happen elsewhere in the country and I am afraid I could not give a blanket answer with respect to this particular problem without looking at the file. If the hon. member would be satisfied to accept a report from me at a later date, I shall be happy to have the matter investigated.

I would appreciate that. It is very serious when a report of this nature is published in a newspaper with a circulation amounting to a few hundred thousand and especially when the author of the article suggests that the new regulations are a racial measure directed at negro entertainers who want to enter Canada. I believe it would be an excellent thing to have the matter clarified.
Without listening to any more detail I would say that such statement is absolute nonsense. We have negro entertainers coming into Canada right across the country from Halifax to Nova Scotia-
Halifax to Vancouver.
Yes, thank you, Vancouver to Halifax. If they are bona fide entertainers and have contracts with Canadian places of entertainment they would have no difficulty.
I hope the hon. member is not suggesting that they would not be admitted to Newfoundland.
Oh, no. I was thinking of the immediate border.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, have there been any changes in the regulations respecting oriental immigration or are any changes contemplated? I am thinking of people in those categories described by the minister as borderline cases. These people do not necessarily

I am afraid I do not understand what it is to which the hon. member refers. Before I resume my place perhaps I may be permitted to indicate to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I now have some tables which I promised to make available to him the other day. If I have the permission of the committee, Mr. Chairman, instead of trying to read these rather voluminous tables, possibly I could place them on Hansard at this time.

The hon. lady was also going to see if she could not supply me with the memorandum which takes the place of that incomprehensible document that she produced last year. Has she reached any conclusion about that yet?
I think that is still to come, Mr. Chairman. I will find out about that. These charts came through first.

One other question; I
think, as far as I recall without checking back in Hansard, these were the only things the hon. lady agreed to produce. If she regards this as a breach of my agreement she does not need to answer this question. There was one question I meant to ask and forgot and it is this. Does the department still refuse to allow persons who are in Canada as visitors to apply for landing while they are inside the country?

Generally speaking, yes, Mr. Chairman, but there are some extenuating circumstances. I do not think I can give a


flat answer to the question. For instance, a person comes in and marries, or comes in to visit a relative and the relative takes ill. Of course, humanitarian principles govern in cases such as these. I do not think I could give my hon. friend a straight answer to his question.
The hon. lady will remember that the first year she was minister she was very rigid about this. I gather from what she says she has learned from experience.
I would not say it was learning from experience so much as it was relaxing in cases where humanitarian principles call for some relaxation.
Perhaps I could say the minister is following a good example.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister about a rather delicate aspect of the immigration problem. Probably every hon. member has been approached by persons in this country with relatives in some other country, and the plaintive quality of their supplication, either in letter form or over the telephone and sometimes in person, takes the form of pleading, offering to do anything to be able to bring their loved one, their family or other persons to Canada. From time to time in discussions with these persons it has been suggested that they wanted to approach their member of parliament and do the thing properly and honestly, but the suggestion has persisted, certainly as long as I have been a member of parliament, that there are people who can fix these things.
Of course, any time this suggestion is made I try to obtain the name. I used to ask for it outright and, of course, the individual concerned would immediately shy away. On several occasions, one within the last year, upon asking about this particular individual who was supposed to be able to fix these things the individual informed me that he had already been asked that question, presumably by somebody in the immigration department, and he had turned over that information. As a matter of fact, in one case he said the mounted police had come and interviewed him almost immediately.
I must say I was greatly impressed with the dispatch with which this investigation was followed up. Certainly, the obvious suggestion conveyed by those persons-those are applicants for friends and family to come to the country-was that this person who had the inside track was getting to somebody within the department. As I say, I was impressed with the fact that they were being pinned down, they were being followed up.

the minister can tell us anything about those investigations? To her knowledge, have any of those types of individuals been apprehended? If so, what has happened to them?

Indian affairs branch-
55. Administration, $792,099.
Does the hon. lady wish to make a statement?

Mr. Chairman, since I last introduced estimates for the Indian affairs branch in this house I have had the privilege of meeting many more Indian Canadians in their far flung home communities. Last September I visited Churchill and talked with Indian people who live on the shores of Hudson bay. A few weeks ago I met others who live on the shores of the Atlantic in historic Cape Breton. Previously I had visited with the great prairie tribes and had met with them at their ceremonial fires. I have also visited the homes of those ancient Canadians who net their livelihood from the deep waters of the Pacific. I mention these things to indicate to hon. members that the conclusions I have arrived at are not the result of merely cursory examination of statistics nor of an isolated visit to a community with a particular local problem, but are born of firsthand knowledge after visiting these Canadians in their communities from sea to sea.
1 would not deny that the problems of these, our oldest Canadians, are many and difficult. Indeed they are, and their solution will require understanding, imagination and the best and wises decisions that we who legislate can bring to bear. And here let me say that I have high hopes that exhaustive examination of the social and economic status of the Indians now being undertaken by the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons will point the way to both legislative changes and desirable programs.
Be that as it may, I am convinced, and I am sure hon. members are of like mind, that it is our bounden duty to ensure that Canadians of the Indian race are given the opportunity of sharing fully in the national life of this country. This will be denied


them unless they are given the training, academic and technical, to fit them for our increasingly complex and highly industrialized economy. I have recently stated outside this house the desirability of new Canadians possessing these skills from a point of view of their own good as well as that of Canada. It is, therefore, our duty to ensure that the oldest of our many Canadian races are granted these necessary skills.
The estimates now before the committee bear witness to our intentions to accept this obligation. Hon. members will note that almost $29 million, over 58 per cent of the total Indian affairs appropriation, is proposed for educational purposes. This continued expansion of the Indian educational program is reflected not only in the number of pupils receiving education but also in the scope of the courses which are being made available for Indian students. Preliminary reports indicate that the number of Indian pupils receiving an education has now reached the figure of approximately 42,500 of whom more than 10,000 are enrolled in non-Indian schools, universities, teachers' colleges, commercial and trade schools. The statistics for the year ended December 31, 1960 are not yet available but it is anticipated that at the present rate of increase during the fiscal year 1961-62 pupils attending such institutions will number in excess of 11,500.
In September, 1960 a revision of teachers' salaries was approved. The increase in the requirements for teachers' salaries for the 1961-62 fiscal year, which is approximately 4 per cent higher than the current fiscal year, is to provide for this increased salary scale. The department currently employs 1,351 teachers of whom 123 are of Indian status, or 9.1 per cent of the total teaching staff. It is my hope that this percentage will steadily increase.
The program of organizing education committees composed of Indian band members has continued a fairly rapid expansion. Last year I reported that 19 such committees were in existence. To date this number has increased to 25. These committees have been established in the following regions:	in
British Columbia, 6; in Alberta, 3; in Saskatchewan, 9; in Ontario, 5; in Quebec, 1; and in the maritimes, 1.
The department awarded 18 new scholarships during the fiscal year 1960-61 to outstanding students, the total of which amounted to $17,910, an increase of one in the number of awards and of $3,600 in the total value.
Provision is made for the construction of 109 new classrooms of which 40 are for the replacement of existing units and 40 new staff units, with a total estimated cost of

construction amounting to $5,500,000. In addition, provision is made for financial contributions toward a share of the construction cost of provincial schools in connection with the joint education of Indian and non-Indian pupils in 26 localities. During the current year 15 agreements for joint education of Indian pupils have been completed, with government contributions totalling approximately $1,100,000. The department has now completed 98 agreements with various provincial and territorial school boards in connection with the joint education of Indian and non-Indian pupils.
During the current fiscal year the program of repairs and upkeep of Indian schools was accelerated and had the additional attraction of providing for more winter employment. It is expected that an amount of approximately $483,000 will be expended by March 31, 1961, over and above the amount originally provided for this purpose.
In addition to the regular school program, the department has continued its work in the adult education field. During the year 1959-60 the total enrollment was approximately 1,300 with the greatest number enrolled in literacy and homemaking courses. In this regard the upgrading courses institute an interesting innovation in our adult education program this year. Under these schemes young Indian men and women who have left school are given short concentrated courses in English, mathematics and social orientation to prepare them for commercial, trade training and employment. Much interest and enthusiasm have been indicated so that now we have over 150 participants in such courses in Edmonton, Regina, Prince Albert and at Muncey. It is very apparent that the young Indian adult is becoming increasingly aware of the necessity of formal training.
An obvious extension of our responsibilities to Canadians of the Indian race is to ensure that, once skills have been attained, equal opportunities exist for them in the economic life of Canada. Through the new economic development division, which came into operation about a year ago, it has been possible to place added emphasis on the distinction between relief assistance on the one hand and the promotion of employment opportunities on the other. In the field of agriculture, assistance has generally been provided on a repayable basis. The program of lending cattle on a rotational basis to selected Indians in the western provinces has aroused considerable interest during the past year, and the current estimates include provision for a very substantial increase in livestock expenditures.

Under the employment placement program, with excellent co-operation from the national employment service, the total number of selected Indians placed in regular employment in urban centres since April, 1957 has now risen to over 700, of whom 270 were placed during the year ended November 30 last. These are for the most part young Indians qualified for their jobs. They are in a very real sense pioneers in the process of integration; and the department has continued the policy of careful selection with this in mind and with a view to promoting good and lasting relationships with employers.
Rural and seasonal placements in which placement and field officers participated totalled over 8,500 from April, 1957 to November, 1960 and included nearly 4,000 individuals placed during the last year. These figures do not, of course, include Indians who have obtained employment independently or with the assistance of their local agency superintendent.
One of the problems in encouraging young Indians to take advantage of vocational training and employment opportunities has been, in many cases, their lack of education and social development. This problem was thoroughly reviewed at a meeting of administrative, educational and placement staff at Edmonton in October last. As a result, additional courses providing academic upgrading and social orientation have been initiated or are planned at several points in western Canada.
A regional placement officer was appointed to Fort Smith, Northwest Territories, in September, 1960, bringing the total of such specialists to nine. A new appointment for the Yukon Territory is expected shortly, and the estimates include provision for four additional appointments at London, Ontario, The Pas, Manitoba, Calgary, Alberta, and Prince George, British Columbia.
While economic development activities are extending into new fields the fact must not be forgotten that many Indians still depend on hunting, trapping and fishing for their livelihood and will continue to do so. In areas where fishing companies operate, the department assists Indian fishermen by providing equipment when required on a repayable basis, generally through deductions from sales of fish. In other areas the department has organized fishing operations on a project basis and provided supervision equipment, ice houses and other facilities. These operations serve as a training ground for Indian fishermen.
As in the past, Indian trappers have been grubstaked where required. The demands for this type of assistance tend to increase when other employment opportunities diminish. The

In carrying out the various administrative programs of assistance the department has not overlooked the vital importance of research to meet the needs of tomorrow. An economist was appointed in October, 1960, as an economic development officer, to initiate surveys and studies and to co-ordinate activities of this nature carried out on our behalf or independently by other agencies. Several economic surveys are now in the process of being organized.
In introducing Indian affairs estimates last year I mentioned that a record total of 1,465 homes had been built on reserves and that 228 units had been started. Final records are not yet available for the current year but it is clear that we can expect another very successful year. Members will recall that to help meet the shortage of houses on many reserves and to provide employment during the winter months an additional sum of $200,000 was provided for this purpose in the supplementary estimates passed by the house on December 20 last.
I think hon. members will be particularly interested and pleased to note provision of $100,000 under the heading of loans, investments and advances to make possible housing loans to individual Indians on reserves. The purpose of this relatively small sum is merely to launch the program which will be introduced as soon as possible in the fiscal year 1961-62 in a few pilot areas. The purpose of these funds is to make loans available to Indians who earn a sufficient income to assume such obligations but who cannot secure credit from other lending institutions because of restrictions upon the use of real property situated on reserves as security.
The appropriation for housing is maintained at the same level as in previous years, which as members will recall this government doubled in 1958. These funds will provide grants and subsidies in addition to loans for families whose income is not sufficient to enable them to meet their housing requirements from present or future income.
In regard to welfare assistance, it will be recalled that the former ration system was discontinued in April of 1959. The change in procedure and the increased scale of benefits provided placed a good deal more responsibility upon Indian bands and upon individual members of these bands. Since I last reported to the house on this subject the number of bands whose needy members receive assistance by cheque has increased from 20 per cent to 40 per cent. A particularly interesting


development this year has been the negotiation of an agreement with the province of Manitoba. Under this agreement the federal and provincial governments share in the costs of a community development program which the province has launched in an effort to improve the social and economic standards in a number of communities with both Indian and Metis populations.
I should like to comment also, as a matter of general interest, upon the fact that 16 bands representing 74 per cent of the Indians in southern Ontario and 10 bands representing 13 per cent of the Indians in northern Ontario are now administering their own welfare assistance programs on exactly the same basis as municipalities in Ontario. This has been possible through amendments to the Ontario general welfare assistance act and the application of section 68 of the Indian Act.
All persons in these reserves apply to the band welfare administrator in non-Indian municipalities. Assistance is provided by this administrator from funds established in the band bank account. An 80 per cent subsidy, 50 per cent of which represents the federal share under the Unemployment Assistance Act agreements, is paid direct to the bands by the province. Under this program bands administer their own program, pay the normal municipal share of the costs, and deal directly with the province.
This progressive measure is being energetically pushed forward by the province of Ontario in co-operation with the Indian affairs branch. Discussions with other bands in the province are now under way, and it is expected that this program will be extended in the near future. Much has been and is being accomplished in works of a capital nature designed to improve the economy and conditions on populated reserves.
Perhaps the most important aspect of this program has been the extensive construction of roads which are needed, not only for the development of Indian community life but are most essential in providing the Indian population with access to neighbouring municipalities where advantage may be taken of the opportunity for employment and the means of earning a better livelihood. The importance of roads to the educational program, especially on the larger reserves, must not be overlooked. It is only by the provision of better roads that greater use of school bus transportation can be made to ensure that more Indian children attend classes regularly in the schools operated by the department as well as municipal schools where such arrangements are in effect.
It is interesting to note the co-operation received from provincial governments by the branch in its roadbuilding program in many

areas. The payment of provincial subsidies or straight sharing of project costs by the provincial departments concerned have resulted in more and better roads being developed and, in many instances, having these joined up with important provincial and municipal road systems. A continued high level of expenditure on these capital works is anticipated in the new year.
In these introductory remarks I have endeavoured to make it clear that these estimates are designed to meet our needs if certain clearly defined objectives are to be attained: First, a continued acceleration of our educational program so that Indian youth will be assured the opportunity of a full academic life and the opportunity of learning those skills which are necessary tools with which to work and progress in our national life; second, the development of projects designed to enable him to take full advantage of knowledge so gained; and, third, the improvement of home and community facilities so that he may walk securely among us as a fellow citizen blessed with a proud heritage.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is a great advantage to the committee to have had the quite comprehensive survey that has just been given by the minister. I should like to thank the hon. lady for the neat way in which she summarized what she felt to be the most important aspects of the work of the department. I am very happy to see that there seems to be no difference between us that the most important part of the work of the Indian affairs branch is in the field of education. It is incomparably more important than anything else. I am very glad also to observe that it is realized more and more that education does not stop at the age of 16.
One of the most tragic features-I think I have mentioned this on several occasions before but it does no harm to mention it again-of Indian affairs administration for many years was the lack of any provision for those young people who came out of residential schools and who went back to the reserves. These people often came from broken homes and were orphans at the age of 16. They returned to the reserve because there was no place for them to go and, in some cases, they were quite disoriented from their band. This was something that certainly should not have been allowed to continue even as long as it did.
We do know that after the war the government began to repair the damage which had resulted from the neglect of the war years, and there was so much to do in so many directions that it could not all be done at once. It is reassuring, and I am sure it is true, to find that today no Indian who can 90205-6-135

Yes, that is right.

I think this has been true since the days when Mr. Harris was the minister, and the provision of the scholarships, with which I was associated when I was minister, was just another stage in the development. I think it was more a moral change than anything else in that it seemed to me that the scholarships established a recognition of merit. Before the scholarships were established the Indians were not denied the education that they were capable of taking. The gratifying thing is that there are more, not as many as we would hope perhaps, of these young Indians who finish high school and who go into universities, more who go into technical schools and, more recently, into vocational training.
It is very encouraging also to find, if I understood the hon. lady correctly, that there has been an increasing interest on the part of adult Indians, particularly the younger adults, in securing vocational training of one kind or another. I must say I should like to look again at what the hon. lady said about the placement service to see whether there is an adequate reflection in the placement of the increased educational training. I would hope there is, but of course we do recognize that in the present circumstances employment is not quite as easy to get as it was a few years ago when people were coming to beg us to provide Indians for various occupations. We know it is not quite so easy to get jobs today.
I think it would be interesting, when we are considering these estimates tomorrow in somewhat more detail, to have the minister tell us about some of the areas in which there is an increasing amount of regular employment being provided for the Indians off the reserves and particularly in the northern and frontier areas. It seems to me that they are much better adapted to provide really stable employees than are many of the people who drift into these areas from the more settled parts of the country and who also quite often drift out quickly afterwards.
I intend to make a request of the minister and I should like to give her notice of this request now. Some time tomorrow I intend to ask the minister whether she could have a computation made and could give it to us, first of all, giving the latest available figure of the total Indian population which I believe is growing. I presume a D.B.S. estimate was made.

I could give it right away.

I think it would perhaps be better to have all this information together. What I should like to have is this. I should like to know approximately how much the federal government is spending not just in the Indian affairs branch but also adding in the amount in the Indian health branch.
I am not responsible for that.

I know the minister is not responsible for this matter but in order to get a figure that would not be a discredit to the government of the country, I think it would be desirable to add the two together just to find out per capita what we are spending on the Indians. I think this would be of interest to the people of Canada generally. I think it is the kind of information that it would be desirable to give. If the minister gives only the figures for her own department that would be a gross underestimate of what really is being done by the Canadian people.
I can speak to my colleague.
I could do the arithmetic myself for the minister but I have not as much technical assistance as she has.
That is not the way we heard it.

If I could get the assistance of the hon. member for Port Arthur perhaps I could do these problems in arithmetic myself. I think perhaps I could do them, but I am appealing to the minister and to her sense of collective responsibility in making this particular request.
I was also greatly interested in what the minister said about the administration of welfare. I recall that in 1957 we took the first tentative steps in a few pilot reserves to pay relief in cash and to leave it to the Indians to make their own decisions as to the way in which they would spend that money. I know this was done with a certain amount of misgiving on the part of many of those who were associated with that decision. From what the minister has said I gather that this procedure had turned out well and that it is being adopted to an increasing extent. I was also interested in-and I think I shall have a few more questions to ask about it-this arrangement that is being made with the government of Ontario for the administration of relief through municipalities.
I should also be greatly interested to hear in more detail about this new agreement in


Manitoba which was already, of course, being foreshadowed by work that was being done in the legislature as much as five years ago by a legislative committee. As a matter of fact the department lost an extremely useful member of the citizenship branch who went to the government of Manitoba when I was minister in order to start the planning of this work. I am prompted to make one other observation and then I am going to sit down because I should like the hon. member for Skeena to have a few minutes.
Oh, oh.

There seems to be a marked difference between the attitude toward Indians of provincial governments in those provinces in which the Indians have the vote and that in those in which they do not have the vote.

The graciousness of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate overwhelms me. I was sure that with his vast store of knowledge and his great interest in this matter he would be making perhaps more than one speech on the item.
I make no promises.

In the few moments at my disposal may I express the appreciation of all of us in the effective opposition of the comprehensive statement of the minister earlier in opening up these estimates. We think that quite correctly she has put her finger, as well as has the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, on the whole question of the acculturation or the integration of Indians or the mutual interest amongst Indians and non-Indians. I refer to the field of education.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that at an earlier stage when we were debating the establishment of a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Indian affairs we also dealt with this matter. My particular point then was that education is a thing upon which we must rest our hopes and in which we must place our faith with regard to having our Indian people take the longest possible step toward a decent way of life and respectable living.
Incidentally, while I am on the subject of the joint committee, may I say this. I cannot for the life of me understand the long delay in calling that committee or why that committee has not been called since it has been established. I hope this difficulty will perhaps be overcome within the next two or three days or at the beginning of the week so that this all-important committee can get down to studying the intricacies of this particular problem to the end that it might come up this session with some decent recommendation.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.
Perhaps I could ask the house leader what the government is planning for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we will carry on with the estimates that come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; that is to say we shall conclude Indian affairs. Then there are some other items such as national gallery, film board, archives and national library which would be passed, I hope tomorrow.
For the guidance of the house, I might just say this. When you consider the fact that the estimates of 20 departments are to come before the house, it is advisable early in the session to allocate the time so that we are not rushed in our deliberations toward the conclusion of the session. About six hours have been devoted to this particular department. If these estimates are concluded tomorrow we will carry on then with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. The forecast for next week, which I underline is subject to change, runs as follows. On Monday and Tuesday there would be a supply motion, the subject matter being in the hands of the opposition. Wednesday, Thursday and Friday would be devoted to government business.
Unless something occurs over which I have no control it is expected that on Wednesday
Business of the House
we will deal with the motion in the name of the Minister of Transport to set up the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping followed by the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport to amend the Canadian National Railways Act. That resolution is No. 5 on today's order paper.
The estimates for next week will be announced, I imagine, on Monday or Tuesday of next week. It depends on the progress we make tomorrow.

I might perhaps draw the attention of the leader of the house to the fact that there was an implication to be drawn from what the Prime Minister said that the estimates of the Department of Labour would be taken next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Prime Minister suggested there was an opportunity on the supply motion for the subject which concerns the opposition to be discussed. A good deal depends on that. If the spokesman for the opposition will tell me what the subject is to be for Monday and Tuesday, then perhaps I could announce whether the estimates of the Department of Labour will be considered next week.
It being three minutes after ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
